# Performance, v3: an OLTP benchmark on PostgreSQL
Source: https://anantharajuc.github.io/QueryAPIGate-website/Guide.dc.html?d=PERFORMANCE_V3

# Performance, v3: an OLTP benchmark on PostgreSQL

**The short answer.** One gunicorn worker (as in the Docker image) in front of PostgreSQL, serving a saved query by
primary key to 32 concurrent callers:

| | v0.41.0 | `main` (unreleased 0.42) | `main` with the metadata cache |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests a second | 682 | 743 | 875 |
| One caller at a time, p50 | 1.43 ms | 1.38 ms | 1.05 ms |
| With a governed key (masking and a table allow-list) | 171 | 693 | 802 |

- **The governance features cost about 7% now.** A key with masking and a table allow-list is about 4× faster than
  in v0.41.0.
- **One process serves 730-875 requests a second.** p99 stays at about 4 ms up to 75% of that, then climbs.
- **More processes add throughput.** Eight workers reached 2,165-2,727 requests a second on four physical cores.
- **PostgreSQL is never the limit here.** At most it used 2 of the 4 hardware threads it had.
- **The remaining cost of a call** is about 1 ms of Python (logging alone takes a fifth of it), plus its round
  trips to PostgreSQL. A call on `main` makes 7: 3 to QueryAPIGate's own store and 4 to the data database. With the
  metadata cache, it makes 4. Over a real network, those round trips dominate.

For MySQL - one server, a database per microservice, per-user queries joining across them - see
[Performance on MySQL](PERFORMANCE_MYSQL_V1.md).

**How to read the numbers.** Every comparison is the median of 5 interleaved rounds, with its min-max range. A
difference counts as real only when the two ranges don't overlap. The cold-path test and the profile are single long
runs, marked where they appear. This page replaces [Performance, v2](PERFORMANCE_V2.md): [What changed from
v2](#what-changed-from-v2) lists what its review found and what was done about each point.

## Contents

- [Method](#method)
- [Results](#results)
- [Where the time goes](#where-the-time-goes)
- [Sizing](#sizing)
- [What to do with this](#what-to-do-with-this)
- [What changed from v2](#what-changed-from-v2)
- [Limits](#limits)
- [Run it yourself](#run-it-yourself)

## Method

### Two sessions

The results come from two sessions on the same machine, with the same harness and settings:

| Session | When | Blocks | `/health` floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2026-10-23, 20:59-23:24 | pgbench, throughput, single-call latency, cold path, access log, profile | 1,934-2,296 req/s |
| B | 2026-10-24, 08:45-11:08 | open loop, scale-out, network, mixed and hot rows, threads, round trips | 1,959-2,258 req/s |

Session A also ran the session-B blocks with 3 rounds each, for v2. A review of v2 pointed out that 3 rounds is too
few for the comparison rule below, so session B reran those blocks with 5. Only session B's numbers are used for
them here. The two sessions agree where they overlap: one worker at 32 callers served 743 lookups a second on `main`
in session A, and 730 in session B.

### The machine, and how it was kept steady

One laptop: an Intel i7-12700H with 6 performance cores (CPUs 0-11, two threads each) and 8 efficiency cores (CPUs
12-19), 32 GB of memory, Ubuntu with kernel 6.8.

- **On AC power,** with the power profile and the CPU's energy preference both set to `performance`. Turbo stays
  on, because turning it off needs root. Its effect is measured below.
- **Each part on its own cores**, so they don't take CPU from each other:

  | Part | CPUs | How |
  |---|---|---|
  | QueryAPIGate (gunicorn) | 0-7: four performance cores, both threads of each | `taskset -c 0-7` |
  | PostgreSQL | 8-11: two performance cores | `docker run --cpuset-cpus 8-11` |
  | Load generator (oha) and pgbench | 12-19: the efficiency cores | `docker run --cpuset-cpus 12-19` |

- **No proxy in the path.** The gateway reaches PostgreSQL at the container's own address, not through Docker's
  published port, whose userland proxy is another unpinned process copying every byte.
- **A floor before and after every block:** 10 s of `/health` on one worker, the same work every time, so a machine
  that changed speed shows up. Both sessions sagged about 10% in their last hour, after about 90 minutes of load.
  That's why every table compares only within its own block, where the builds take turns.
- **The load generator was never the bottleneck.** It used at most 0.79 of its 8 cores, at 2,700 requests a second.

### Turbo, measured

The busiest gateway core's clock was sampled every 2 s of every run. It ranged from 2.4 to 4.4 GHz overall, but that
range is between blocks: with 8 busy workers, the cores run at a lower all-core turbo. Within a cell - the same
build, call and setting - the clock varied by only ±1% (5th to 95th percentile, over 184 runs).

Turbo still explains the outliers. Within cells, a run's clock and its throughput correlate (r = 0.59), and the rare
fast rounds are clock spikes. In session A, a v0.41.0 round ran at 4.09 GHz against its cell's 3.65, and served 11%
more. That's the reason for 5 rounds and the range rule: one fast round widens a range rather than moving a median.

### When a difference counts

Builds take turns in an order rotated each round (A B C, then B C A, then C A B), so none always runs first,
warmest or coolest. A difference counts as real only when the two cells' ranges don't overlap.

How often does that rule call a difference real when there isn't one? If two builds were really the same, every
ordering of their 2n results would be equally likely, and the ranges would be clear in 2 of the C(2n, n) orderings.
For 5 rounds that's 2 in 252, under 1%. For 3 rounds it's 2 in 20, 10%, which is why v2's 3-round blocks were rerun.
This page makes about 40 such comparisons, so expect perhaps one of the narrow ones to be luck. The large ones
aren't.

### The builds

| Label | What | Commit |
|---|---|---|
| **v0.41.0** | the 0.41.0 release | `f61d4ed` |
| **main** | `main` after the performance work in #88, unreleased - what 0.42 will ship | `c9b15c2` in session A, `99db30b` in session B: the same `queryapigate/` code; only docs changed between them |
| **main+cache** | the same, with `QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL=5` | as main |

Each is exported from git (`git archive`) and run as the Docker image runs it: gunicorn with the `gthread` worker,
8 threads, the access log on, everything else at its default (so v0.41.0 has a pool of 5, `main` a pool of 8).

Software: Python 3.12.3, gunicorn 26.2.0, Flask 3.1.1, psycopg2 2.9.10, sqlglot 25.34.1, PostgreSQL 16.15
(`postgres:16`), oha 1.16.0 pinned by digest
(`ghcr.io/hatoo/oha@sha256:3ec3dbf549ea197793482d47a6324797411406bbf438c2fe8b91f244ec641a2f`).

### The database

pgbench's TPC-B-like schema at scale 100 (`pgbench -i -s 100`), 1.5 GB, fully in memory
(`shared_buffers=2GB`, `max_connections=300`, `synchronous_commit=on`):

| Table | Rows | Columns | Key |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pgbench_accounts` | 10,000,000 | `aid integer`, `bid integer`, `abalance integer`, `filler character(84)` | primary key `aid` |
| `pgbench_branches` | 100 | `bid integer`, `bbalance integer`, `filler character(88)` | primary key `bid` |
| `pgbench_tellers` | 1,000 | `tid integer`, `bid integer`, `tbalance integer`, `filler character(84)` | primary key `tid` |
| `pgbench_history` | 0 | `tid`, `bid`, `aid`, `delta integer`, `mtime timestamp`, `filler character(22)` | none |

QueryAPIGate's own store - keys, saved queries, connections, run history - is a second database, `qagstore`, in the
same PostgreSQL, as `QUERYAPIGATE_DATABASE_URL`.

### The calls and the keys

Three saved queries on one connection, `oltp`, called with a random id on every request:

| Saved query | SQL | Called as |
|---|---|---|
| `account` - a **lookup** | `SELECT aid, bid, abalance FROM pgbench_accounts WHERE aid = :aid` | `/q/account?aid=` 1 to 9,999,999 |
| `account_page` - a **100-row page** | `SELECT a.aid, a.abalance, b.bid, b.bbalance FROM pgbench_accounts a JOIN pgbench_branches b ON b.bid = a.bid WHERE a.aid BETWEEN :start AND :start + 99 ORDER BY a.aid` | `/q/account_page?start=` 1 to 999,999`&page_size=100` |
| `deposit` - a **write** | `UPDATE pgbench_accounts SET abalance = abalance + :delta WHERE aid = :aid` | `/q/deposit?aid=` 1 to 9,999,999`&delta=` 1 to 9 |

| Key | Grants |
|---|---|
| **plain** | `{"queries": ["account", "account_page"], "connections": []}` |
| **governed** | the same, plus `"allowed_tables": ["pgbench_accounts", "pgbench_branches"]` and `"mask": [{"column": "*.abalance", "action": "hash"}]` |
| **writer** | `{"queries": ["deposit"], "connections": [], "allow_writes": true, "allowed_write_ops": ["update"]}`, on a server with `QUERYAPIGATE_ALLOW_WRITES=1` |

[`benchmarks/oltp.py`](https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/blob/main/benchmarks/oltp.py) creates all of
them through the Management API. Across the two sessions, every one of the 12 million requests that completed
returned 200. Requests still in flight when a run's time was up aren't counted either way.

### The load

- **Closed loop**, for throughput: `oha -c N` keeps N callers, each sending its next request when the last one
  answers. 30 s per run, after a 5 s warm-up at 8 callers that also fills the pool and the governance caches.
- **Open loop**, for latency against load: `oha -q R --latency-correction` sends R requests a second whatever
  happens, and measures each request from when it should have been sent. That avoids coordinated omission, where a
  closed loop under-reports latency at saturation because a slow answer delays the next request. The rates are 25%
  to 110% of capacity, 20 s each, with 128 connections available. Capacity is measured first in the same block:
  5 closed-loop rounds at 32 callers.

### What is recorded for each run

- **Throughput and latency:** requests a second, the success rate and every status code; p50, p90, p99 and p99.9,
  from oha's own percentiles.
- **CPU, in cores**, for each part:
  - the gateway's, from `/proc` (master and workers);
  - PostgreSQL's, from its container's cgroup (`cpu.stat`);
  - the load generator's cores, from `/proc/stat`.
- **Transactions per request**, on the store and on the data database, from `pg_stat_database`. These are exact
  for 30 s runs. For exact *statement* counts, `log_statement = 'all'` was turned on for a few hundred requests (see
  [Round trips](#round-trips-per-call)).
- **The machine's state:** the busiest gateway core's clock, and the CPU package temperature (65-100 °C).

The data is in
[`benchmarks/results/oltp-postgres-2026-10-23/`](https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/tree/main/benchmarks/results/oltp-postgres-2026-10-23)
(session A, with the cold-path per-second latency and the py-spy profiles) and
[`benchmarks/results/oltp-postgres-2026-10-24/`](https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/tree/main/benchmarks/results/oltp-postgres-2026-10-24)
(session B). Each has `results.jsonl`, one line per run, and `results.md`, every table, generated by
`benchmarks/oltp_report.py`.

## Results

### The database on its own

pgbench from the load generator's cores, 5 rounds of 10 s (session A):

| Workload | Clients | Transactions a second | Average latency |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary-key read (`pgbench -S`) | 1 | 38,289 (37,465-39,586) | 0.026 ms |
| Primary-key read (`pgbench -S`) | 32 | 112,321 (96,140-123,670) | 0.285 ms |
| TPC-B: three updates, a select, an insert | 32 | 12,970 (12,617-15,293) | 2.5 ms |

A lookup costs PostgreSQL 0.03 ms on two cores. Everything a call through QueryAPIGate takes beyond that is the
gateway and its round trips.

### One process, 32 callers

Session A. **Cached** is `main` with the metadata cache on.

| Call | | v0.41.0 | main | Cached |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lookup, plain key | req/s | 682 (679-686) | 743 (736-746) | 875 (869-876) |
| | p99 | 55.8 ms | 54.1 ms | 45.1 ms |
| Lookup, governed key | req/s | 171 (171-172) | 693 (691-694) | 802 (800-806) |
| | p99 | 223 ms | 57.1 ms | 49.9 ms |
| 100-row page | req/s | 596 (595-598) | 639 (638-642) | 738 (737-740) |
| | p99 | 64.8 ms | 61.4 ms | 52.7 ms |
| Write | req/s | 682 (679-683) | 738 (733-743) | 875 (872-881) |
| | p99 | 56.9 ms | 53.9 ms | 45.9 ms |

All the ranges are clear of each other:

- **main against v0.41.0:** +7 to 9% for plain keys, from reading the store less (below); +304% for a governed
  key, from the masking and table-check caches.
- **Cached against main:** +16 to 19%, on every call.
- **The gateway used 1.2 cores for one worker:** one for Python, the rest for the threads' I/O. PostgreSQL used
  0.2-0.4.

### One caller at a time

The latency of a single call (session A):

| Call | | v0.41.0 | main | Cached |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lookup, plain key | p50 | 1.43 ms (1.43-1.44) | 1.38 ms (1.35-1.42) | 1.05 ms (1.04-1.06) |
| | p99 / p99.9 | 2.1 / 3.0 ms | 2.2 / 3.1 ms | 1.7 / 2.4 ms |
| Lookup, governed key | p50 | 6.00 ms (5.79-6.06) | 1.48 ms (1.46-1.51) | 1.20 ms (1.16-1.20) |
| | p99 / p99.9 | 7.6 / 13.6 ms | 2.4 / 3.3 ms | 1.9 / 2.5 ms |

- **For one plain caller, main and v0.41.0 overlap:** three fewer store reads don't show at this speed. The cache's
  -24% does.
- **A governed call** went from 6 ms to 1.5.

### Latency against offered load

The lookup, open loop and latency-corrected, 20 s per rate (session B). Capacity, measured first, was 730 (720-797)
requests a second for main and 862 (840-872) cached. The cells are p50 / p99 / p99.9:

| Offered | main | Cached |
|---|---|---|
| 25% | 2.0 / 3.0 / 11.0 ms | 1.5 / 2.3 / 10.5 ms |
| 50% | 1.6 / 2.8 / 8.4 ms | 1.1 / 2.1 / 9.8 ms |
| 75% | 1.5 / 3.8 (3.2-4.1) / 13.5 ms | 1.2 / 3.4 (3.3-4.6) / 15.0 ms |
| 90% | 1.7 / 11.1 (7.6-12.9) / 21.7 ms | 1.2 / 8.7 (6.3-11.6) / 19.0 ms |
| 100% | 1.9 / 22.7 (18.3-67.2) / 27.8 ms | 1.6 / 17.2 (15.2-23.6) / 21.8 ms |
| 110% | 664 / 1,584 / 1,607 ms; 744 of 802 served | 305 / 1,276 / 1,296 ms; 893 of 948 served |

- **p50 stays flat** right up to capacity. **p99 holds at about 4 ms to 75%,** then climbs: about 3× at 90%, 6×
  at 100%.
- **Past capacity, a queue builds.** Latency reaches seconds within the 20 s run. Requests that were still queued
  when the time was up are neither served nor failed in these counts.
- **Real capacity is a little higher than measured.** At 110%, more was served than the closed-loop capacity: 744
  against 730, and 893 against 862. The open loop's 128 connections get 2-4% more out of a worker than 32 callers
  do. So each row's real load sits a few percent below its label, and the 75% planning figure below errs on the safe
  side.
- **The lightest loads show a higher p99.9 than 50%:** at a trickle, an idle core clocks down between requests.

### Scale-out

Workers in one gunicorn (each a process, as each container would be), 64 callers (session B):

| Workers | Lookups req/s: main | Lookups: Cached | Writes: main | Writes: Cached |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 734 (733-739) | 869 (866-871) | 732 (729-733) | 863 (844-866) |
| 2 | 1,196 (1,193-1,202) | 1,441 (1,431-1,445) | 1,188 (1,185-1,190) | 1,430 (1,428-1,434) |
| 4 | 1,716 (1,709-1,722) | 2,112 (2,104-2,124) | 1,706 (1,701-1,710) | 2,087 (2,078-2,094) |
| 8 | 2,215 (2,127-2,264) | 2,727 (2,638-2,801) | 2,165 (2,096-2,229) | 2,651 (2,552-2,683) |

| Workers | p99, lookups: main / Cached | Gateway cores | Lookups/s per gateway core: main / Cached | PostgreSQL cores: main / Cached |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 103 / 88 ms | 1.2 | 612 / 736 | 0.30 / 0.17 |
| 2 | 74 / 59 ms | 2.3-2.4 | 501 / 622 | 0.56 / 0.31 |
| 4 | 66 / 69 ms | 4.6-4.7 | 367 / 463 | 1.04 / 0.56 |
| 8 | 139 / 92 ms | 7.2 | 307 / 377 | 1.65 / 0.92 |

- **The cache's lead is clear at every size:** +18% to +23%.
- **Throughput grows with processes, but not linearly here,** and the table shows why. Requests a second per
  gateway core fall from 612 at 1 worker to 307 at 8. All 8 workers share CPUs 0-7, which are only four physical
  cores. From 4 workers on, the workers share cores' second hyperthreads, and a hyperthread is worth far less than a
  core. Containers on their own cores, or their own hosts, would scale better than this. This run can't show by how
  much.
- **The cache halves PostgreSQL's work.** At 8 workers it used 1.65 cores without the cache and 0.92 with it. Most
  of PostgreSQL's load was QueryAPIGate's own store, not the queries.
- **p99 at 8 workers rises,** and its range widens (84-184 ms without the cache): 8 processes and their threads
  contend for 8 hardware threads.

### Threads per worker

One worker, the lookup, 32 callers (session B):

| Threads | req/s | p99 | Gateway cores |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 788 (782-792) | 51.7 ms | 0.87 |
| 2 | 843 (842-851) | 47.5 ms | 1.12 |
| 4 | 777 (772-778) | 51.0 ms | 1.19 |
| 8 | 735 (734-737) | 54.5 ms | 1.20 |

All four ranges are clear of each other.

- **Two threads are best on this workload:** one runs Python while the other waits on the database.
- **Beyond two, throughput falls.** Eight threads, the Docker image's setting, are 13% slower than two, and 7%
  slower than a single thread. They compete for Python's global interpreter lock and, the profile shows, for the
  logging module's lock.
- **That applies to fast queries only.** Threads are for calls that wait: slow queries, `?stream=true` exports,
  and `/events` connections that stay open. See [Sizing](#sizing).

### The cold path: every 60 seconds

One 150 s run of the lookup at 8 callers per key (session A, a single run each), with each request's duration from
gunicorn's access log (`%(D)s`):

| Key | Requests | p50 | p99 | p99.9 | p99.99 | Slowest |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| governed | 106,741 | 9.25 ms | 14.66 ms | 19.2 ms | 73.7 ms | 146.9 ms |
| plain | 115,314 | 8.58 ms | 13.57 ms | 16.9 ms | 20.9 ms | 26.0 ms |

The log starts with the server, so the 5 s warm-up comes first. In a typical second the slowest request took 17 ms;
three seconds stand out:

- **t=1 s, 147 ms:** the very first governed calls, which read the connection's schema and trace the statement for
  masking for the first time.
- **t=61 s and t=121 s, 76 and 74 ms:** the same work again, 60 seconds later each time, when QueryAPIGate's copy of
  the schema expires.

So a governed key pays about 75 ms every minute, more on the very first call. Only the few requests that arrive
while it happens wait, so it shows at p99.99, not at p99.9. The plain key has no table check or masking to redo, and
no spikes.

### The access log

`main`, the lookup, 32 callers, gunicorn's access log on and off (session A):

| Access log | req/s | p50 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| on (the Docker image's default) | 736 (735-739) | 43.0 ms | 54.4 ms |
| off | 785 (782-792) | 40.2 ms | 51.7 ms |

- **The access log costs 7%.**
- **QueryAPIGate also logs two lines of its own for each request,** at INFO, which can't be turned off. The profile
  below puts all logging at a fifth of the gateway's CPU.

### A database across a network

netem on the database container delays everything PostgreSQL sends by 0.5 ms
(`tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 0.5ms`; ping goes from 0.04 to 0.56 ms). That's about a same-zone cloud
round trip. The lookup, session B:

| | v0.41.0 | main | Cached |
|---|---|---|---|
| One caller: req/s | 133 (132-134) | 162 (161-168) | 270 (267-273) |
| One caller: p50 | 7.57 ms | 6.24 ms | 3.65 ms |
| 32 callers: req/s | 674 (670-753) | 735 (734-741) | 855 (852-874) |

- **One caller pays for every round trip.** At 0.5 ms each, a call on `main` went from 1.4 to 6.2 ms.
  - Fewer store reads made `main` 21% faster than v0.41.0.
  - The cache made it 67% faster again, and cut single-call latency by 41%, to 3.65 ms.
- **With 32 callers, round trips overlap,** and the CPU is the limit again, so the builds come out in the same order
  as without a delay.
- **v0.41.0's range overlaps `main`'s here,** in both sessions. One of its five rounds ran at 753 requests a second,
  at 4.09 GHz against about 3.62 for the other four. Its median is 9% below `main`'s.
  - Both times, that was the block's first run, straight after the 10 s `/health` floor, on a CPU with turbo headroom
    to spend.
  - The rotation starts each part of the block with the same build, so v0.41.0 got that first slot twice. A
    harness fix would carry the rotation across the parts, or run one unrecorded warm-up first.
- **This is a simulation:** one-way delay, no packet loss or jitter. The next section uses it to count round trips.
  It isn't a cloud measurement.

### Mixed reads and writes, and hot rows

`main` (session B):

| Workload | req/s | p50 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reads (24 callers) and writes (8 callers) at once | 548 (546-549) + 181 (181-182) | 43.3 / 43.6 ms | 54.4 / 54.9 ms |
| Writes on 10 million accounts (32 callers) | 734 (733-736) | 43.1 ms | 54.4 ms |
| Writes on 99 hot accounts (32 callers) | 738 (735-740) | 42.9 ms | 53.9 ms |

- **Mixing reads and writes changes nothing:** they share the process's capacity in proportion, 729 a second in
  total.
- **Writes on 99 hot rows cost the same as on 10 million.** One worker sends at most 8 at once, so PostgreSQL's row
  locks never queue long enough to show. With many workers, or a slow transaction, they would.

## Where the time goes

### Round trips per call

**Counted.** `log_statement = 'all'` was turned on for each database, then 100 calls were made after a warm-up:

| Statements per call | v0.41.0 | main | Cached |
|---|---|---|---|
| Store, plain key or writer | 7: 5 reads, 2 inserts | 3: the key, the query, the connection | 0.1: history, in batches |
| Store, governed key | 8 | 4 | 1: the masking hash key |
| Data database, any call | 4: `BEGIN READ ONLY`, `SET LOCAL statement_timeout`, the query, `ROLLBACK` | 4 | 4 |
| **Round trips a call waits for** (the history inserts happen in the background) | **9** | **7** | **4** |

**Measured.** Single-call p50 at 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 ms of netem delay, 3 rounds per point (session B). The slope of
latency against the delay is the number of round trips a call waits for. psycopg2 on its own, sending a known 1 or
4 statements, calibrates the method:

| | +0 ms | +0.5 ms | +1 ms | +2 ms | Slope | Round trips (slope ÷ 1.15) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| psycopg2, 1 statement | 0.03 | 0.63 | 1.19 | 2.33 | 1.15 | 1 |
| psycopg2, the 4 statements a query sends | 0.06 | 2.44 | 4.68 | 9.36 | 4.60 | 4.0 |
| v0.41.0 | 1.42 | 7.60 | 12.47 | 22.66 | 10.46 | 9.1 |
| main | 1.43 | 6.24 | 10.01 | 18.75 | 8.58 | 7.5 |
| Cached | 1.05 | 3.70 | 5.84 | 10.59 | 4.72 | 4.1 |

- **Under netem, one round trip costs 1.15 ms per ms of delay,** not 1. Bare psycopg2 shows the same factor, at 1
  statement and at 4. It is netem's per-packet overhead, not the gateway.
- **Divided by it, the measured round trips match the counted ones:** 9.1 against 9, 7.5 against 7, 4.1 against 4.
  The statement log missed nothing. (A v2 review had asked whether it did: v2's raw 0.5 ms figures implied 1-3
  round trips more than counted.)
- **History and events** are written in batches of up to 500 by a background thread, about once a second, so a
  call doesn't wait for them.
- **The governed key reads the masking hash key on every call,** even with the cache on.
- **A query takes four round trips to the data database:** a transaction, its time limit, the statement, then the
  rollback (or commit, for a write).

### The CPU

py-spy at 200 samples a second across the worker's threads, during one 30 s run of the lookup at 32 callers
(session A). Each sample is counted under the innermost frame that falls in one of these categories:

| Where the samples fall | main | Cached |
|---|---|---|
| Store layer: queries, decoding rows, checks | 28.2% | 13.4% |
| Logging: the access log and QueryAPIGate's own lines | 18.4% | 20.4% |
| gunicorn, sockets, HTTP | 16.8% | 21.0% |
| Data query: the driver and the pool | 12.3% | 15.4% |
| Flask and Werkzeug | 9.9% | 11.9% |
| QueryAPIGate's request handling | 4.6% | 5.6% |
| History writer thread | 3.0% | 3.7% |
| Authentication, limits, quotas, metrics | 2.5% | 2.8% |
| SQL checks, parameters, masking | 1.7% | 1.9% |
| JSON | 1.3% | 2.6% |
| Other | 1.3% | 1.3% |

The busiest single frames say more:

- **`logging` lock acquisition: 8-10%.** Eight threads write log lines through one handler, and wait on its lock.
  That's the same contention that makes more threads slower.
- **`store.refuse_store_access`: 7-10%.** A safety check that a connection doesn't point at QueryAPIGate's own
  SQLite file. It resolves file paths (`os.path.realpath`, several system calls) on every call - even for a
  PostgreSQL connection, which has no file to point at. With the cache on, it's the largest single cost in the store
  layer.
- **The store's `execute`: 17% in main, gone with the cache.** That's the three reads.
- **gunicorn's per-request worker heartbeat (`workertmp.notify`): 3%.**

## Sizing

A worker has two limits, and it reaches whichever comes first:

- **CPU.** About 550 calls a second per worker, or 650 with the metadata cache, for fast OLTP calls at p99 of about
  4 ms. That's 75% of the capacity above. Every millisecond of Python a call costs beyond this page's lookup lowers
  it.
- **Waiting.** A worker holds at most as many calls at once as it has threads. A call waits for its query, plus its
  round trips (7 on `main`, 4 cached), each taking the network's round-trip time. So a worker serves at most:
  threads ÷ (query time + round trips × round-trip time) calls a second.

**Workers needed** = the larger of (calls a second ÷ the CPU figure) and (calls a second ÷ the waiting figure), plus
one to lose without falling over.

Two examples, at a 0.5 ms network round trip:

| Calls | CPU figure | Waiting figure, 8 threads | What limits a worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| A 0.03 ms lookup, as on this page | 550 a second | 8 ÷ (0.03 + 7 × 0.5 ms) = about 2,270 a second | CPU: fewer threads would do (see [Threads](#threads-per-worker)) |
| A 20 ms report query | 550 a second, or fewer | 8 ÷ (20 + 3.5 ms) = about 340 a second | Waiting: give it more threads, as long as CPU allows |

These are planning figures from one machine and one query shape. Measure your own queries at 75% of what you plan to
serve before you commit to a number.

## What to do with this

**For running QueryAPIGate:**

- **Size with the rule above,** then measure your own queries, which will usually cost more than these.
- **Turn on `QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL`** if a few seconds' delay is acceptable for a change made on another
  instance to reach this one. A worker then serves 16-23% more, PostgreSQL does half the work, and across a network a
  single call takes 41% less time. The trade-off is explained in [PERFORMANCE.md](PERFORMANCE.md#the-metadata-cache).
- **Match threads to your queries:**
  - For fast queries, `--threads 2` beats the default 8 by 15% here.
  - Keep 8 or more if calls wait on slow queries, exports or `/events`.
- **Turn off gunicorn's access log** if a proxy in front already logs requests: +7%.
- **Scale with processes on their own cores.** A hyperthread gave about half a core here.

**For QueryAPIGate itself** - findings worth an issue each, in the order I'd take them:

1. **Fewer round trips per query.** Set `default_transaction_read_only` and `statement_timeout` once per pooled
   session, or send `BEGIN` and `SET LOCAL` in one round trip with the query.
   - That takes 4 round trips down to 1 or 2.
   - At a 0.5 ms round trip, saving 3 of them takes about 1.7 ms off every call: 6.2 to about 4.5 ms on `main`, and
     3.7 to about 2 ms cached.
2. **Skip `refuse_store_access`'s path checks for server databases.** Only SQLite, DuckDB and H2 open a file. That
   would save 7-10% of CPU on every PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse and Trino call.
3. **Cache the masking hash key.** It's read on every governed call, and almost never changes.
4. **Make logging cheaper:** a setting to skip the per-request INFO lines, or a queue handler so threads don't
   wait on one lock. That's up to a fifth of the CPU.
5. **Refresh the schema and masking trace in the background,** before they expire. Then no governed call waits the
   extra 75 ms each minute, or the 147 ms on its first call.

## What changed from v2

A review of v2 rated it 4.1 out of 5. What it raised, and what v3 did about it:

| Raised | Done |
|---|---|
| "Halved single-call latency": 6.24 → 3.69 ms is -41%, not half, and another section says 40% | -41% throughout |
| "No caller waits 60-140 ms every minute": the recurring spikes are about 75 ms, and 147 ms is the first call | "About 75 ms every minute, more on the first call", with why the first spike is at t=1 |
| v1's 2× gap credited to power alone, though v2 also pinned cores and removed Docker's proxy | All three are credited (below) |
| "Every number is a median with its range", though some tables showed medians only | Ranges in every comparison table; the single long runs are marked |
| 3 rounds give a 10% chance of a false "clear" | Every 3-round block was rerun with 5 (under 1%), and the rule's odds are stated in the method |
| The threads result cleared by 3 req/s, in a 3-round block | With 5 rounds, every threads range is clear: 2 threads are best, and 8 trail 1 by 7% |
| Counted round trips didn't explain the network result | A calibrated slope test: they match once netem's 1.15× per-trip overhead is accounted for |
| Closed-loop "capacity" was below what was served at 110% | Capacity is now measured in the same block; the 2-4% gap is stated |
| The clock range was recorded but never used | ±1% within cells; turbo spikes explain the outlier rounds |
| Load generator CPU not recorded | Recorded per run: at most 0.79 of its 8 cores |
| The short answer named 4 round trips but not the 3 to the store | 7 on `main`, 4 cached |
| Unfinished requests at 110% might be read as part of "every request returned 200" | Stated: requests still queued when a run ended are counted neither way |
| Run time stated two ways | One figure, under [Run it yourself](#run-it-yourself) |

**Carried over from v2's corrections to v1:**

- **The store transactions per call.** v1 said about 5.5 before its changes and 2.6 after. Counted exactly, it's 7
  statements before (5 reads and 2 inserts) and 3 after. PostgreSQL holds back an idle session's statistics for up to
  10 seconds, and v1 read them about 2 seconds after its run ended.
- **v1's PostgreSQL throughput was about half of this page's:** 368 requests a second for `main` against 743 here.
  The code was the same. Three things changed at once: the laptop went from battery and a power-saving profile to AC
  and `performance`; every part got its own cores; and the gateway stopped reaching PostgreSQL through Docker's
  userland proxy. No run changed one at a time, so this page doesn't say how much each was worth. The power state is
  likely most of it, because `/health`, which doesn't touch PostgreSQL, doubled as well.

## Limits

- **One machine.** The gateway, the database and the load generator share it, on separate cores but one memory bus
  and one cooling system. Four physical cores for the gateway limit what scale-out can show.
- **No TLS, no load balancer or proxy, and no Redis,** so there are no shared rate limits. Each of them would add
  to the cost of a call.
- **The network is simulated,** one way, without jitter or loss.
- **Uniform random keys.** Real traffic is skewed. Hot rows were tested for writes, but not as a skewed read
  pattern, which would matter to a cache in front of the database.
- **Small results only:** one row, or a page of 100. Large results, `?stream=true`, the MCP server and the other
  databases weren't measured.
- **p99.99 and the slowest requests** come only from the 150 s runs. Elsewhere, 30 s runs give about 20,000 samples,
  enough for p99.9.
- **py-spy counts samples of threads it considers active,** and a thread waiting for the interpreter lock can count.
  So the shares say where the time is spent, not exactly how much each part would save.
- **The first run after a floor gets a turbo burst.** A block's rotation starts its first round with the same build in
  each part of the block, so that build gets the burst more often - see the network section.
- **No soak or failure tests.** Hours at 75% load, which would show memory, pool and history-writer behaviour over
  time, weren't run. Neither was losing PostgreSQL or a worker mid-run.

## Run it yourself

You need Docker, `taskset`, and QueryAPIGate's server, PostgreSQL and masking dependencies in the Python that runs
the script. py-spy is optional, for the profile:

```bash
pip install -e ".[server,postgres,flow]" py-spy
python benchmarks/oltp.py --out /tmp/qag-oltp setup all teardown     # about 3 hours 45 minutes
python benchmarks/oltp_report.py /tmp/qag-oltp/results.jsonl         # writes results.md beside it
```

- **Cores and refs:** `--gateway-cpus`, `--db-cpus` and `--load-cpus` take `taskset`-style lists; check your own
  machine's layout with `lscpu -e`. `--base` and `--head` choose the two git refs (v0.41.0 and `origin/main` by
  default).
- **Fewer blocks:** name them instead of `all`, e.g. `setup env b1 b2 teardown` - each block's docstring says what it
  measures. `--smoke` runs every block for 2 s, to check the setup in about 10 minutes.
- **Plug in first.** Check `powerprofilesctl get` and the AC state; the `/health` floors will show it if you
  forgot.
- **What it leaves behind:** `teardown` removes the database container and its data volume, about 2 GB.


# Performance on MySQL, v1: microservice databases, per-user queries
Source: https://anantharajuc.github.io/QueryAPIGate-website/Guide.dc.html?d=PERFORMANCE_MYSQL_V1

# Performance on MySQL, v1: microservice databases, per-user queries

**The case.** One MySQL server holding six databases, one per microservice. Read-only queries look up one user at a
time and join across those databases. No column masking. QueryAPIGate sits in front, with one connection and one
read-only MySQL user.

**The short answer.** One gunicorn worker, as in the Docker image, with 32 concurrent callers:

| Query (databases it joins) | MySQL directly, 32 threads | v0.41.0 | `main` | `main` + metadata cache |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `customer` - one user's row (crm) | 75,420/s | 609 | 676 | 777 |
| `order_status` - TPC-C Order-Status (crm, orders) | 25,063/s | 532 | 579 | 651 |
| `order_history` - last orders with item names (crm, orders, catalog) | 19,116/s | 552 | 604 | 677 |
| `payments` - the user's payments (crm, billing) | 38,136/s | 605 | 671 | 770 |
| `profile` - the user with district and warehouse (crm, org) | 50,026/s | 609 | 677 | 772 |
| `stock_level` - TPC-C Stock-Level (org, orders, inventory) | 5,343/s | 583 | 642 | 725 |

- **A call adds about 1.2-1.5 ms** to a query MySQL answers in 0.03-0.42 ms. That's the gateway's Python plus 3 round
  trips to MySQL. Every one of the 9.65 million requests returned 200.
- **One worker serves 580-780 of these a second.** The gateway, not MySQL, is the limit: MySQL could serve 8-110
  times more, and at 8 workers it used at most 2.5 cores.
- **`main` is 9-11% faster than v0.41.0, and the metadata cache adds 12-15% more,** on every query. That's
  +22-27% in all.
- **Fewer threads are faster.** For a fast lookup, one thread per worker beat the Docker image's eight by 28%.
- **Skewed traffic plus a 30 s response cache:** when a few users are much busier than the rest (Zipf), 59% of calls
  came from the cache, throughput rose 23%, and MySQL got 58% fewer statements.
- **One security gap:** on MySQL, a key's table allow-list can't tell `crm.customer` from `billing.customer`. Keep
  services apart with MySQL's own grants until that's fixed. See [Isolating services](#isolating-services).

**How to read the numbers.** Each cell is the median of 5 interleaved rounds, with its min-max range in the detailed
tables. A difference counts as real only when two ranges don't overlap. The method is the one in
[Performance, v3](PERFORMANCE_V3.md#method), applied to MySQL.

- [Results](#results)
- [Where the time goes](#where-the-time-goes)

- [Disk: the event log](#disk-the-event-log)

## Method

### The machine

The same laptop as [Performance, v3](PERFORMANCE_V3.md#the-machine-and-how-it-was-kept-steady): an Intel i7-12700H,
on AC power, with the `performance` power profile and energy preference. One session, 2026-10-24 19:33 to
2026-10-25 00:44 (5 h 11 min). Each part ran on its own cores:

| Part | CPUs |
|---|---|
| QueryAPIGate (gunicorn) | 0-7: four performance cores, both threads |
| MySQL 8.4.13 | 8-11: two performance cores |
| The load generator (oha), sysbench | 12-19: the efficiency cores |

The gateway reached MySQL at the container's own address, over TLS. mysql-connector negotiates TLS by default, and
sysbench was run with `--mysql-ssl=REQUIRED`, so the direct numbers pay the same encryption cost.

A `/health` floor before and after every block stayed between 1,919 and 2,298 requests a second (−12% to +6% of its
median), with the low end in the m6-m8 blocks. The CPU package ran at 66-100 °C. The load generator never used more
than 0.63 of its 8 cores.

### The builds

| Label | Commit |
|---|---|
| **v0.41.0** | `f61d4ed` |
| **v0.42.0** | `647ab6f` |
| **main** | `3a92e5d`: 0.42.0 plus #95 (the store-file check skipped for server databases, the masking key cached, `QUERYAPIGATE_LOG_REQUESTS`) |
| **main + cache** | the same, with `QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL=5` |

Each runs as the Docker image does: gunicorn's `gthread` worker, 8 threads, the access log on. QueryAPIGate's own
store is SQLite in its home directory - the single-instance default - except in the store comparison below.

### The data: TPC-C, split into six databases

[go-tpc](https://github.com/pingcap/go-tpc) loaded TPC-C at **20 warehouses**: 1.9 GB, which fits MySQL's 4 GB
buffer pool. The data is TPC-C's, and two of the queries are TPC-C's read-only transactions, but this isn't the
TPC-C benchmark, and its numbers aren't TPC-C results.

The nine tables were then moved into six databases, one per service, with `RENAME TABLE`:

| Database | Tables | Rows |
|---|---|---|
| `org` | `warehouse`, `district` | 20, 200 |
| `crm` | `customer` | 600,000 - the users |
| `orders` | `orders`, `new_order`, `order_line` | 600,000, 180,000, 6,000,000 |
| `catalog` | `item` | 100,000 |
| `inventory` | `stock` | 2,000,000 |
| `billing` | `history` (payments) | 600,000 |

TPC-C defines no index for looking a customer's payments up, so `billing.history` got one on its customer key, as the
payments service would. The row counts are MySQL's estimates as recorded with the results.

QueryAPIGate has **one connection**, as user `qag`, which has `SELECT` on the six databases and nothing else.
MySQL resolves `crm.customer JOIN orders.orders` within one session, so every cross-database join is one query.

### The queries

Six saved queries. Each `user` query takes a customer by TPC-C's key (`w`, `d`, `c`). The full SQL is in
[`benchmarks/tpcc_mysql.py`](https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/blob/main/benchmarks/tpcc_mysql.py).

| Query | What it does | Tables joined |
|---|---|---|
| `customer` | One customer's row by primary key | 1 |
| `order_status` | TPC-C Order-Status: the customer, their latest order and its lines | 3 |
| `order_history` | The customer's last orders with each item's name, 50 rows | 4 |
| `payments` | The customer's last 20 payments | 2 |
| `profile` | The customer with their district and warehouse | 3 |
| `stock_level` | TPC-C Stock-Level: distinct items below a stock threshold among a district's last 20 orders | 3, a range and `COUNT(DISTINCT)` |

One key, `reader`, may run all six; there are no masking rules.

### The load

- **Customers are drawn from 600,000,** uniformly by default. The skew block draws them from a Zipf distribution
  (s = 1.0), so that a few customers are very busy. Ranks map through a fixed shuffle, so the hot customers are
  spread across warehouses.
- **Requests come from files of 200,000 URLs,** through oha's `--urls-from-file`. Because the files are generated
  rather than taken from a URL regex, the user ids really are uniform.
- **Closed loop** for throughput: 30 s runs after a 5 s warm-up. **Open loop** for latency under load, latency
  corrected, at 25-110% of capacity measured in the same block.
- **MySQL directly:** sysbench sends each query's SQL, with the same random parameters, in autocommit: one statement
  per call, as a service with its own connection would. sysbench's standard `oltp_read_only` runs on its own tables
  for reference.
- **What every run records:** throughput, latency percentiles, every status code; CPU for the gateway, MySQL and the
  load generator; MySQL's `Questions` counter, for statements per request (exact and immediate); and the clock and
  temperature.

## Results

### MySQL on its own

| Test | 1 thread | 32 threads |
|---|---|---|
| sysbench `oltp_read_only` (transactions/s) | 1,695 (1,683-1,710) | 4,425 (4,415-5,544) |
| `customer` | 28,303/s, p50 0.03 ms | 75,420/s |
| `order_status` | 12,053/s, p50 0.08 ms | 25,063/s |
| `order_history` | 9,618/s, p50 0.10 ms | 19,116/s |
| `payments` | 18,479/s, p50 0.05 ms | 38,136/s |
| `profile` | 21,793/s, p50 0.04 ms | 50,026/s |
| `stock_level` | 2,373/s, p50 0.42 ms | 5,343/s |

Each `oltp_read_only` transaction is 16 statements. On two cores, MySQL answers these per-user joins in tens of
microseconds. `stock_level`, with its range and `COUNT(DISTINCT)`, is the only one near half a millisecond.

### One worker, 32 callers

| Query | v0.41.0 | v0.42.0 | main | main + cache |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `customer` | 609 (609-615) | 643 (641-649) | 676 (672-679) | 777 (772-778) |
| `order_status` | 532 (529-537) | 558 (555-560) | 579 (577-582) | 651 (642-652) |
| `order_history` | 552 (550-553) | 580 (579-583) | 604 (601-607) | 677 (675-678) |
| `payments` | 605 (601-606) | 638 (635-642) | 671 (666-672) | 770 (761-771) |
| `profile` | 609 (607-610) | 641 (639-642) | 677 (676-679) | 772 (768-777) |
| `stock_level` | 583 (581-586) | 613 (612-616) | 642 (640-644) | 725 (719-728) |

All the ranges are clear of each other:

- **v0.42.0 over v0.41.0: +5-6%.** MySQL gets no help from 0.42's PostgreSQL-focused changes, but it does from
  reading the store less.
- **main over v0.42.0: +4-6%,** from #95: the store-file check is skipped for a server database like MySQL, and
  the masking key read is gone. Over v0.41.0, main is +9-11%.
- **The metadata cache adds +12-15% on top of main,** for +22-27% over v0.41.0 in all.
- **The gateway used 1.1-1.3 cores, and MySQL 0.08-0.47.** At p99, main is at 57-67 ms and the cache at 48-57 ms:
  that's 32 callers queueing for one worker, not slow queries.

The heavier the query, the less the gateway matters to it. `stock_level` runs at 12% of MySQL's direct rate through
one worker, `customer` at 1%. A worker's ceiling is its Python, whatever the query.

### One caller at a time

The p50 of a single call, with what the gateway adds to the same query sent directly:

| Query | MySQL directly | v0.41.0 | main | main + cache | The gateway adds (main + cache) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `customer` | 0.034 ms | 1.28 ms | 1.22 ms | 1.16 ms | +1.12 ms |
| `order_status` | 0.081 ms | 1.54 ms | 1.46 ms | 1.40 ms | +1.32 ms |
| `stock_level` | 0.417 ms | 1.76 ms | 1.70 ms | 1.64 ms | +1.22 ms |

- **A call costs about 1.1-1.5 ms more through the gateway,** whatever the query: a fixed cost, not a percentage.
- **p99 stays under 2.4 ms** in every build, and p99.9 under 3.3.
- **For one caller, v0.42.0 and v0.41.0 overlap** on two of the three queries. main is 4-5% faster than v0.41.0, and
  the cache another 4-5%.

### Latency under load

`order_status`, open loop and latency-corrected. Capacity was 583 (581-584) calls a second for main and 652
(649-654) with the cache. Each cell is p50 / p99 / p99.9:

| Offered | main | main + cache |
|---|---|---|
| 25% | 2.1 / 3.1 / 20.2 ms | 2.0 / 2.9 / 12.3 ms |
| 50% | 1.8 / 2.5 / 10.5 ms | 1.7 / 2.3 / 16.9 ms |
| 75% | 1.6 / 5.0 (3.0-8.8) / 29.8 ms | 1.5 / 4.6 (3.0-12.1) / 21.2 ms |
| 90% | 1.6 / 5.5 (4.6-9.0) / 19.2 ms | 1.7 / 9.0 (6.7-10.9) / 19.9 ms |
| 100% | 1.9 / 17.0 / 27.1 ms | 1.9 / 17.8 / 24.6 ms |
| 110% | 450 / 857 / 864 ms; 619 of 640 served | 597 / 1,366 / 1,383 ms; 673 of 716 served |

- **p50 stays near 2 ms right up to capacity.** p99 is 3 ms to half load, about 5 ms at 75%, and 17 ms at 100%.
- **p99 varied more between rounds here than on PostgreSQL** (3.0-8.8 ms at 75%), so plan at 75%, as there.
- **p99.9 sits at 10-30 ms even at light load,** where PostgreSQL's was 6-15. It's a few slow calls in a thousand,
  not a trend.

### More workers

64 callers:

| Workers | `order_status`: main | main + cache | `stock_level`: main | main + cache | MySQL cores (`stock_level`, cache) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 583 (581-585) | 650 (647-654) | 639 (636-642) | 724 (721-726) | 0.47 |
| 2 | 968 (963-972) | 1,114 (1,111-1,116) | 1,044 (1,041-1,048) | 1,213 (1,207-1,219) | 0.90 |
| 4 | 1,363 (1,357-1,378) | 1,639 (1,633-1,646) | 1,476 (1,471-1,485) | 1,763 (1,758-1,774) | 1.64 |
| 8 | 1,873 (1,805-1,936) | 2,114 (2,092-2,202) | 1,989 (1,914-2,032) | 2,236 (2,213-2,254) | 2.47 |

- **Throughput grows with workers, and the cache's lead holds at every size** (+11% to +20%).
- **Growth flattens past 2 workers.** Calls a second per gateway core fall from 469 at one worker to 262 at eight,
  for the reason v3 found: the eight workers share four physical cores' hyperthreads.
- **MySQL is far from its limit.** At 2,236 `stock_level` calls a second it used 2.5 of its 4 hardware threads, and
  for `order_status` 0.6.

### Threads per worker

One worker, 32 callers:

| Threads | `customer` (0.03 ms) | `stock_level` (0.42 ms) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **865 (864-879)** | 630 (624-633) |
| 2 | 823 (817-827) | **772 (769-777)** |
| 4 | 722 (721-727) | 683 (681-688) |
| 8 | 676 (675-677) | 642 (636-646) |

All the ranges are clear. **The faster the query, the fewer threads it wants:**
- `customer`, at 0.03 ms in MySQL, is fastest with one thread: **28% faster than the default eight.**
- `stock_level`, at 0.42 ms, is fastest with two: 20% faster than eight. One thread is too few for it, because it
  then waits on MySQL with nothing else to do.

That fits the sizing rule below. Threads only help while calls spend real time waiting.

### Skewed users and the response cache

`order_status` at 32 callers. `order_status_cached` is the same query with `cache_ttl: 30`. Each run starts a fresh
process, so the cache starts empty:

| Customers | Query | Calls/s | p50 | Cache hits | MySQL statements per call |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| uniform | `order_status` | 582 (578-583) | 54.7 ms | - | 2.00 |
| uniform | `order_status_cached` | 537 (535-541) | 59.3 ms | 5% | 1.90 |
| Zipf | `order_status` | 581 (580-582) | 54.7 ms | - | 2.00 |
| Zipf | `order_status_cached` | **717 (714-719)** | **44.3 ms** | **59%** | **0.83** |

- **Skewed traffic is where a response cache pays.** With a few users making most of the calls, 59% were answered
  from the cache: +23% throughput, and 58% fewer statements reached MySQL.
- **Uniform traffic doesn't benefit.** With 600,000 equally likely users, only 5% of calls repeat within 30 s, and
  storing the 95% that never get reused costs 8%.
- **Skew alone changes nothing without the cache:** 581 against 582. MySQL's buffer pool already holds everything.

### A database across a network

netem delays everything MySQL sends by 0.5 ms (about a same-zone cloud round trip). `order_status`:

| | v0.41.0 | v0.42.0 | main | main + cache |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One caller: p50 | 3.58 ms | 3.58 ms | 3.55 ms | 3.39 ms |
| One caller: calls/s | 280 (275-284) | 279 (278-281) | 283 (282-287) | 293 (287-295) |
| 32 callers: calls/s | 421 (420-427) | 436 (434-444) | 450 (450-451) | 489 (486-490) |

- **A 0.5 ms hop adds about 2.1 ms to a call:** 3 round trips (see below), at 0.6 ms each under netem.
- **The builds barely differ for one caller.** All four make the same 3 round trips to MySQL, and the store, on local
  SQLite here, is off the network.
- **With 32 callers, throughput falls 22% (main),** from 579 to 450. Waiting on the network holds a thread for
  longer, and 8 threads cover less of it.

### The store across the network

Here the network matters. QueryAPIGate's own store on local SQLite, against PostgreSQL across the same 0.5 ms hop,
which is what several instances behind a load balancer share. One caller, `order_status`:

| Store | main | main + cache |
|---|---|---|
| SQLite, local | 3.52 ms (284/s) | 3.39 ms (293/s) |
| PostgreSQL, 0.5 ms away | **6.06 ms (166/s)** | **3.43 ms (292/s)** |

- **Without the cache, a store across the network costs 2.5 ms a call,** the 3 reads it makes, and cuts single-caller
  throughput by 42%.
- **With the cache, it costs nothing:** 3.43 ms against 3.39 ms local. For a multi-instance deployment on a shared
  PostgreSQL store, the metadata cache is the difference between those two rows.

## Where the time goes

### Round trips

Counted with MySQL's general log, 100 calls after a warm-up, in every build:

| Statements per call | |
|---|---|
| The query | 1 |
| `ROLLBACK`, when the connection goes back to the pool | 1 |
| **Total, every build** | **2** |

That's half of PostgreSQL's 4. The MySQL driver makes a connection read-only once, when it opens it (`SET SESSION
TRANSACTION READ ONLY`), and sets the time limit only when it changes. So no per-query `BEGIN` or `SET` is needed.

**Measured, there are 3.** Single-call p50 at 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 ms of netem delay; the slope is round trips per call.
mysql-connector on its own, sending a known 1 or 2 statements, calibrates it:

| | +0 ms | +0.5 ms | +1 ms | +2 ms | Slope | Round trips (slope ÷ 1.2) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| mysql-connector, 1 statement | 0.04 | 0.64 | 1.23 | 2.49 | 1.22 | 1 |
| mysql-connector, query + `ROLLBACK` | 0.05 | 1.26 | 2.39 | 4.75 | 2.35 | 2.0 |
| v0.41.0 | 1.27 | 3.30 | 4.94 | 8.57 | 3.64 | 3.0 |
| v0.42.0 | 1.27 | 3.28 | 4.91 | 8.68 | 3.59 | 3.0 |
| main | 1.21 | 3.21 | 4.86 | 8.25 | 3.53 | 2.9 |
| main + cache | 1.16 | 3.06 | 4.78 | 8.48 | 3.66 | 3.1 |

The third round trip isn't a statement, which is why the log doesn't show it. **mysql-connector's `cursor()` pings
the server** (`is_connected()` → `COM_PING`) every time it's called, and QueryAPIGate's MySQL driver makes a new
cursor for every query. Reusing one cursor per pooled connection would save one round trip in three: about 0.6 ms a
call across a 0.5 ms network.

No connections were opened mid-run. MySQL's `Connections` counter didn't move during 10 s of load at 1, 8 or 32
callers, so this isn't reconnecting; the pool holds.

### The CPU

py-spy, 200 samples a second, during 30 s of `order_status` at 32 callers. Each sample is counted under the innermost
frame that falls in a category:

| Where the samples fall | main | main + cache |
|---|---|---|
| Store layer: the key, the query and the connection, read from SQLite | 25.2% | 5.7% |
| Data query: mysql-connector and the pool | 20.7% | 24.9% |
| Logging | 14.0% | 17.3% |
| gunicorn, sockets, HTTP | 13.9% | 17.7% |
| Flask and Werkzeug | 6.7% | 9.2% |
| History writer thread | 5.9% | 6.0% |
| JSON | 4.0% | 6.5% |
| SQL checks, parameters | 3.7% | 5.7% |
| QueryAPIGate's request handling | 3.2% | 4.2% |
| Authentication, limits, quotas, metrics | 2.2% | 2.3% |
| Other | 0.6% | 0.5% |

What the busiest frames show:

- **Even a local SQLite store costs a fifth of the CPU.** Reading the key, the saved query and the connection is
  7.3% + 7.3% + 6.3% of the samples. That's Python's `sqlite3` and JSON decoding, not I/O. The metadata cache takes
  it to 5.7% in all, which is most of its 12-15% gain.
- **`db._target()` takes 3.6-3.8%,** with or without the cache. It re-reads the store's settings from the
  environment on every call; caching it is a small, safe fix.
- **mysql-connector's ping on every `cursor()`** shows as 2.6-3.8%, and its `ROLLBACK` as 3.1-3.6%.
- **Threads waiting on the logging module's lock: 5-9%,** as on PostgreSQL. `QUERYAPIGATE_LOG_REQUESTS=off` (in
  main) removes most of it.

## Isolating services

Six services in one MySQL server raise a question PostgreSQL's case didn't: can a key for one service be kept out of
another's tables? This is the result of checking, not a performance number. A key with
`"allowed_tables": ["customer"]`, ad-hoc SQL, and a decoy `billing.customer` table:

| SQL | Result |
|---|---|
| `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM crm.customer` | 200: allowed, as intended |
| `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM billing.customer` | **200: allowed, though it's another service's table** |
| `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM billing.history` | 403 `table_not_allowed`, as intended |

**On MySQL, the table allow-list matched bare table names** (0.42 and earlier), so `customer` meant `customer` in
any database the connection's user could reach. Only Trino connections matched `catalog.schema.table`.

**Fixed in 0.43:** grants are schema-qualified on every SQL connection, so `customer` means the connection's own
database's `customer`, and `billing.customer` is refused unless granted (the CHANGELOG's Security entry). Keeping
services apart with MySQL's own grants is still the stronger boundary: one MySQL user per service, granted only its
databases, each as its own QueryAPIGate connection, with keys granted only their service's connection. The
integration tests check both.

Saved queries aren't affected. A key granted named queries can only run those queries' SQL, and that SQL is written
by whoever publishes it.

## Disk: the event log

Every call is recorded in the store's event log (ADR 0020), which keeps events for 24 hours by default. In this run,
the single-instance SQLite store took in 10.6 million events in five hours: **6 GB, about 570 bytes a call.** Run
history, by contrast, stays small, because it keeps only the newest 50 runs per saved query version.

So plan the store's disk for the traffic you serve:

| Sustained calls a second | Event log after 24 hours |
|---|---|
| 50 | about 2.5 GB |
| 500 | about 25 GB |
| 2,000 | about 100 GB |

`QUERYAPIGATE_EVENTS_RETENTION_HOURS` shortens how long events are kept, and the disk needed shrinks with it. On a
PostgreSQL store, rows are larger, so expect more.

## Sizing

The rule from [Performance, v3](PERFORMANCE_V3.md#sizing), with MySQL's figures:

- **CPU:** plan on about 440 calls a second per worker for `order_status`-class queries, or 490 with the metadata
  cache. That's 75% of measured capacity, where p99 is around 5 ms. Single-table lookups go about 15% higher.
- **Waiting:** a worker serves at most threads ÷ (query time + 3 round trips × network round-trip time) calls a
  second.
- **Workers needed** = the larger of the two figures divided into your calls a second, plus one spare.

Two examples, with a 0.5 ms network round trip:

| Calls | CPU figure | Waiting figure | Threads to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| A per-user lookup, 0.1 ms in MySQL | 440 a second | 8 ÷ (0.1 + 3 × 0.5 ms) = 5,000 a second | CPU-bound: 1-2 threads beat 8 |
| A 20 ms report query | 440 a second, or fewer | 8 ÷ (20 + 1.5 ms) = 370 a second | Waiting-bound: more threads help |

MySQL won't be what you size first. On two cores it ran these queries 8-110 times faster than one gateway worker
could ask for them. Its limit shows only with many workers on the heavier queries: 2.5 cores at 8 workers on
`stock_level`.

## What to do with this

**For running QueryAPIGate in front of MySQL:**

- **One connection with a read-only user covering the services' databases** works, and joins across them cost no
  more than joins within one. Use one connection per service if the services must be kept apart (see
  [Isolating services](#isolating-services)).
- **Turn on the metadata cache:** +12-15% on one instance, even with the store on local SQLite. With several
  instances on a shared PostgreSQL store, it removes 2.5 ms of store round trips from every call. Its trade-off -
  a change made on another instance takes up to the TTL to arrive - is explained in
  [PERFORMANCE.md](PERFORMANCE.md#the-metadata-cache).
- **For per-user lookups, run 1-2 threads per worker,** not 8: up to 28% more throughput. Keep more for slow queries.
- **Put `cache_ttl` on queries whose callers repeat themselves** - a dashboard a user keeps refreshing, popular
  accounts. Don't put it on queries every user calls once: there it costs 8%.
- **Turn off the per-request log lines** if a proxy already logs requests: `QUERYAPIGATE_LOG_REQUESTS=off`. At these
  rates the log grows by gigabytes an hour: 6.6 GB in this five-hour run.
- **Size the store's disk for the event log:** about 570 bytes a call, kept for 24 hours (see
  [Disk](#disk-the-event-log)).

**For QueryAPIGate itself - new from this run:**

1. **Reuse one cursor per pooled MySQL connection.** mysql-connector pings the server on every `cursor()`; that's 1
   of the 3 round trips a call makes.
2. **Match `schema.table` in MySQL table allow-lists,** as Trino already does. That's a security fix for the
   multi-service case, not a performance one.
3. **Cache `db._target()`:** 3.6-3.8% of the CPU, re-reading environment settings that don't change.
4. **Read-only MySQL connections could autocommit,** which would drop the `ROLLBACK` round trip too. The session
   is already read-only, so it's likely safe, but stored functions need checking first. This belongs in the same
   design note as the PostgreSQL round trips (ADR 0027).

## Limits

- **One machine,** on separate cores. The scale-out is workers sharing four physical cores, not separate hosts.
- **Every query is cheap,** because the 1.9 GB of data sits in MySQL's buffer pool. Real per-user queries that touch
  disk, or take tens of milliseconds, move the limit from the gateway's CPU to waiting. The sizing rule covers that,
  but this run didn't measure it.
- **The network is simulated:** one-way delay, no jitter or loss. No TLS termination, load balancer or Redis in front
  of the gateway.
- **One query shape per run.** Real services mix them. Mixing reads and writes was measured on PostgreSQL (v3), not
  here. Writes weren't measured on MySQL at all.
- **MySQL's general log counts statements, not packets.** The third round trip was found by timing, and explained by
  reading mysql-connector's code.
- **p99.99** wasn't measured: there were no 150 s runs in this session.

## Run it yourself

You need Docker, `taskset`, the [go-tpc](https://github.com/pingcap/go-tpc/releases) binary, and QueryAPIGate's
server, MySQL and PostgreSQL dependencies. py-spy is optional:

```bash
pip install -e ".[server,mysql,postgres]" py-spy
python benchmarks/tpcc_mysql.py --out /tmp/qag-tpcc --go-tpc ./go-tpc setup A B teardown   # about 5.5 hours
python benchmarks/tpcc_mysql_report.py /tmp/qag-tpcc/results.jsonl
```

- **`--out` must be an absolute path.**
- **`setup`** starts MySQL 8.4, loads 20 warehouses (`--warehouses`) in under a minute, moves the tables into the
  six databases and creates the read-only user. **`A`** runs the direct baseline, throughput and single-call blocks;
  **`B`** runs the rest.
- **`--refs`** chooses the builds (v0.41.0, v0.42.0 and `origin/main` by default; the last also runs with the
  metadata cache), and **`--gateway-cpus`, `--db-cpus` and `--load-cpus`** the cores.
- **`--smoke`** runs every block for 2 s to check the setup.
- **`teardown`** removes the containers and their data volumes.
- **Plug the laptop in first,** and check `powerprofilesctl get`.

The 2026-10-24 run is in
[`benchmarks/results/tpcc-mysql-2026-10-24/`](https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/tree/main/benchmarks/results/tpcc-mysql-2026-10-24):
one JSON line per run, every table, and the py-spy profiles.


# Performance, v2: an OLTP benchmark on PostgreSQL
Source: https://anantharajuc.github.io/QueryAPIGate-website/Guide.dc.html?d=PERFORMANCE_V2

# Performance, v2: an OLTP benchmark on PostgreSQL

> **Superseded by [Performance, v3](PERFORMANCE_V3.md).** v3 reruns this page's 3-round blocks with 5 rounds,
> calibrates the round-trip count, adds sizing, and fixes the overstatements a review of this page found. The
> numbers below aren't wrong, but v3's are the ones to use.

**The short answer.** With one gunicorn worker (as in the Docker image) in front of PostgreSQL, a saved query by
primary key at 32 concurrent callers:

| | v0.41.0 | `main` (unreleased 0.42) | `main` with the metadata cache |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests a second | 682 | 743 | 875 |
| One caller at a time, p50 | 1.43 ms | 1.38 ms | 1.05 ms |
| With a governed key (masking and a table allow-list) | 171 | 693 | 802 |

- **The governance features cost about 7% now.** A key with masking and a table allow-list is about 4× faster than
  in v0.41.0.
- **One process serves 740-875 requests a second.** Latency holds until the load reaches about 75% of that.
- **More processes add throughput.** Eight workers reached 2,200-2,700 requests a second on four physical cores.
- **PostgreSQL is never the limit here.** At most it used 2 of the 4 hardware threads it had.
- **The remaining cost of a call** is about 1 ms of Python (logging alone takes a fifth of it), plus 4 round trips
  to the data database for every query. Over a real network, those round trips dominate.

Every number below is the median of 3-5 interleaved rounds with its min-max range. A difference counts as real only
when the two ranges don't overlap. This page replaces the PostgreSQL parts of [PERFORMANCE.md](PERFORMANCE.md), whose
method two reviews found too weak for its comparisons. [What changed from v1](#what-changed-from-v1) lists what
was fixed, and what v1 got wrong.

## Contents

- [Method](#method)
- [Results](#results)
- [Where the time goes](#where-the-time-goes)
- [What to do with this](#what-to-do-with-this)
- [What changed from v1](#what-changed-from-v1)
- [Limits](#limits)
- [Run it yourself](#run-it-yourself)

## Method

### The machine, and how it was kept steady

One laptop: an Intel i7-12700H with 6 performance cores (CPUs 0-11, two threads each) and 8 efficiency cores (CPUs
12-19), 32 GB of memory, Ubuntu with kernel 6.8. In v1, the same code measured 2× apart on different runs. Most of
that was the laptop: on battery, on a power-saving profile, and with nothing pinned, so the scheduler could move
any part onto a slow efficiency core at any moment. This run:

- **On AC power, power profile `performance`,** CPU energy preference `performance`. Turbo stayed on, since turning
  it off needs root.
- **Each part on its own cores,** so they don't take CPU from each other:

  | Part | CPUs | How |
  |---|---|---|
  | QueryAPIGate (gunicorn) | 0-7: four performance cores, both threads of each | `taskset -c 0-7` |
  | PostgreSQL | 8-11: two performance cores | `docker run --cpuset-cpus 8-11` |
  | Load generator (oha) and pgbench | 12-19: the efficiency cores | `docker run --cpuset-cpus 12-19` |

- **No proxy in the path.** The gateway reached PostgreSQL at the container's own address, not through Docker's
  published port, whose userland proxy is another unpinned process copying every byte.
- **A floor before and after every block:** 10 s of `/health` on one worker, the same work every time, so a machine
  that changed speed shows up. Across the 2 h 25 min of the run it stayed between 1,934 and 2,296 requests a second,
  -13% to +3% of its median. The low end came in the last blocks (network, mixed, threads), which compare only
  within themselves. The CPU package ran at
  65-100 °C, and the busiest gateway core's clock was sampled every 2 s of every run (2.4-4.4 GHz). Both are recorded
  per run.

Software: Python 3.12.3, gunicorn 26.2.0, Flask 3.1.1, psycopg2 2.9.10, sqlglot 25.34.1, PostgreSQL 16.15
(`postgres:16`), oha 1.16.0 pinned by digest
(`ghcr.io/hatoo/oha@sha256:3ec3dbf549ea197793482d47a6324797411406bbf438c2fe8b91f244ec641a2f`).

### The builds

| Label | What | Commit |
|---|---|---|
| **v0.41.0** | the 0.41.0 release | `f61d4ed` |
| **main** | `main` after the performance work in #88, unreleased - what 0.42 will ship | `c9b15c2` |
| **main+cache** | the same, with `QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL=5` | `c9b15c2` |

Each is exported from git (`git archive`) and run as the Docker image runs it: gunicorn with the `gthread` worker,
8 threads, the access log on, everything else at its default (so v0.41.0 has a pool of 5, `main` a pool of 8).

### The database

pgbench's TPC-B-like schema at scale 100 (`pgbench -i -s 100`), 1.5 GB, fully in memory
(`shared_buffers=2GB`, `max_connections=300`, `synchronous_commit=on`):

| Table | Rows | Columns | Key |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pgbench_accounts` | 10,000,000 | `aid integer`, `bid integer`, `abalance integer`, `filler character(84)` | primary key `aid` |
| `pgbench_branches` | 100 | `bid integer`, `bbalance integer`, `filler character(88)` | primary key `bid` |
| `pgbench_tellers` | 1,000 | `tid integer`, `bid integer`, `tbalance integer`, `filler character(84)` | primary key `tid` |
| `pgbench_history` | 0 | `tid`, `bid`, `aid`, `delta integer`, `mtime timestamp`, `filler character(22)` | none |

QueryAPIGate's own store - keys, saved queries, connections, run history - is a second database, `qagstore`, in the
same PostgreSQL, as `QUERYAPIGATE_DATABASE_URL`.

### The calls and the keys

Three saved queries on one connection, `oltp`, called with a random id on every request:

| Saved query | SQL | Called as |
|---|---|---|
| `account` - a **lookup** | `SELECT aid, bid, abalance FROM pgbench_accounts WHERE aid = :aid` | `/q/account?aid=` 1 to 9,999,999 |
| `account_page` - a **100-row page** | `SELECT a.aid, a.abalance, b.bid, b.bbalance FROM pgbench_accounts a JOIN pgbench_branches b ON b.bid = a.bid WHERE a.aid BETWEEN :start AND :start + 99 ORDER BY a.aid` | `/q/account_page?start=` 1 to 999,999`&page_size=100` |
| `deposit` - a **write** | `UPDATE pgbench_accounts SET abalance = abalance + :delta WHERE aid = :aid` | `/q/deposit?aid=` 1 to 9,999,999`&delta=` 1 to 9 |

| Key | Grants |
|---|---|
| **plain** | `{"queries": ["account", "account_page"], "connections": []}` |
| **governed** | the same, plus `"allowed_tables": ["pgbench_accounts", "pgbench_branches"]` and `"mask": [{"column": "*.abalance", "action": "hash"}]` |
| **writer** | `{"queries": ["deposit"], "connections": [], "allow_writes": true, "allowed_write_ops": ["update"]}`, on a server with `QUERYAPIGATE_ALLOW_WRITES=1` |

[`benchmarks/oltp.py`](https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/blob/main/benchmarks/oltp.py) creates all of
them through the Management API. Every one of the run's 5.8 million requests returned 200.

### The load

- **Closed loop**, for throughput: `oha -c N` keeps N callers, each sending its next request when the last one
  answers. Each run is 30 s, after a 5 s warm-up at 8 callers that also fills the pool and the governance caches.
- **Open loop**, for latency against load: `oha -q R --latency-correction` sends R requests a second whatever
  happens, and measures each from when it should have been sent. That avoids coordinated omission, where a closed
  loop under-reports latency at saturation because a slow answer delays the next request. Rates of 25%, 50%, 75%,
  90%, 100% and 110% of the build's closed-loop capacity, 20 s each, 128 connections available.
- **Interleaved.** Within a block, every round runs every build (or setting) once, in an order rotated each round -
  A B C, then B C A, then C A B - so none always runs first, warmest or coolest.

### What is recorded for each run

- Requests a second, the success rate and every status code; p50, p90, p99 and p99.9 latency (oha's own
  percentiles).
- **CPU, in cores:** the gateway's from `/proc` (master and workers), PostgreSQL's from its container's cgroup
  (`cpu.stat`), each divided by the run's wall time.
- **Transactions per request** on the store and on the data database, from `pg_stat_database`. These are exact for
  30 s runs; for exact *statement* counts, `log_statement = 'all'` was turned on for a few hundred requests (see
  [Round trips](#round-trips-per-call)).
- The busiest gateway core's clock and the CPU package temperature.

All of it is in
[`benchmarks/results/oltp-postgres-2026-10-23/`](https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/tree/main/benchmarks/results/oltp-postgres-2026-10-23):
`results.jsonl` (one line per run), `results.md` (every table, generated by `benchmarks/oltp_report.py`), the
per-second latency of the cold-path runs, and the py-spy profiles.

## Results

### The database on its own

pgbench from the load generator's cores, 5 rounds of 10 s:

| Workload | Clients | Transactions a second | Average latency |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary-key read (`pgbench -S`) | 1 | 38,289 (37,465-39,586) | 0.026 ms |
| Primary-key read (`pgbench -S`) | 32 | 112,321 (96,140-123,670) | 0.285 ms |
| TPC-B: three updates, a select, an insert | 32 | 12,970 (12,617-15,293) | 2.5 ms |

A lookup costs PostgreSQL 0.03 ms on two cores. Everything a call through QueryAPIGate takes beyond that is the
gateway and its round trips.

### One process, 32 callers

5 rounds of 30 s per cell. **Cached** is `main` with the metadata cache on.

| Call | | v0.41.0 | main | Cached |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lookup, plain key | req/s | 682 (679-686) | 743 (736-746) | 875 (869-876) |
| | p99 | 55.8 ms | 54.1 ms | 45.1 ms |
| Lookup, governed key | req/s | 171 (171-172) | 693 (691-694) | 802 (800-806) |
| | p99 | 223 ms | 57.1 ms | 49.9 ms |
| 100-row page | req/s | 596 (595-598) | 639 (638-642) | 738 (737-740) |
| | p99 | 64.8 ms | 61.4 ms | 52.7 ms |
| Write | req/s | 682 (679-683) | 738 (733-743) | 875 (872-881) |
| | p99 | 56.9 ms | 53.9 ms | 45.9 ms |

All the ranges are clear of each other:

- **main against v0.41.0:** +7 to 9% for plain keys, from reading the store less (below); +304% for a governed
  key, from the masking and table-check caches.
- **Cached against main:** +16 to 19%, on every call.
- **The gateway used 1.2 cores for one worker:** one for Python, the rest for the threads' I/O. PostgreSQL used
  0.2-0.4.

### One caller at a time

The latency of a single call, 5 rounds of 30 s:

| Call | | v0.41.0 | main | Cached |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lookup, plain key | p50 | 1.43 ms (1.43-1.44) | 1.38 ms (1.35-1.42) | 1.05 ms (1.04-1.06) |
| | p99 / p99.9 | 2.1 / 3.0 ms | 2.2 / 3.1 ms | 1.7 / 2.4 ms |
| Lookup, governed key | p50 | 6.00 ms (5.79-6.06) | 1.48 ms (1.46-1.51) | 1.20 ms (1.16-1.20) |
| | p99 / p99.9 | 7.6 / 13.6 ms | 2.4 / 3.3 ms | 1.9 / 2.5 ms |

For one plain caller, main and v0.41.0 overlap: three fewer store reads don't show at this speed. The cache's
-24% does. A governed call went from 6 ms to 1.5.

### Latency against offered load

The lookup, open loop, latency-corrected, 3 rounds of 20 s per rate. Capacity is each build's closed-loop rate above
(743 and 875 requests a second):

| Offered | main: p50 / p99 / p99.9 | Cached: p50 / p99 / p99.9 |
|---|---|---|
| 25% of capacity | 2.0 / 2.9 / 12.0 ms | 1.5 / 2.3 / 7.8 ms |
| 50% | 1.6 / 2.7 / 6.1 ms | 1.2 / 2.0 / 8.7 ms |
| 75% | 1.5 / 3.5 / 13.6 ms | 1.2 / 3.4 / 14.0 ms |
| 90% | 1.6 / 7.9 / 15.6 ms | 1.2 / 12.2 / 19.4 ms |
| 100% | 1.7 / 18.4 / 25.3 ms | 1.7 / 15.0 / 23.3 ms |
| 110% | 411 / 1,379 / 1,396 ms - served 765 of 816 | 347 / 1,047 / 1,062 ms - served 917 of 962 |

- **p50 stays flat** right up to capacity. **p99 holds under 4 ms to 75%,** then climbs: 2× at 90%, 5× at 100%.
- **Past capacity, a queue builds.** Latency goes to seconds within the 20 s run, and only the capacity's worth of
  requests is served.
- **For capacity planning,** that means about 75% of the closed-loop number: about 550 requests a second per worker
  without the cache, 650 with it, for p99 under 4 ms.
- The lightest loads show a higher p99.9 than 50%: at a trickle, an idle core clocks down between requests.

### Scale-out

Workers in one gunicorn (each a process, as each container would be), 64 callers, 3 rounds of 30 s:

| Workers | Lookups req/s: main / Cached | Writes req/s: main / Cached | p99 lookups: main / Cached | Gateway cores | PostgreSQL cores: main / Cached |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 747 / 878 | 742 / 873 | 99 / 86 ms | 1.2 | 0.29 / 0.17 |
| 2 | 1,214 / 1,472 | 1,202 / 1,448 | 69 / 62 ms | 2.4 | 0.56 / 0.31 |
| 4 | 1,742 / 2,156 | 1,734 / 2,114 | 67 / 61 ms | 4.6 | 1.04 / 0.59 |
| 8 | 2,241 / 2,741 | 2,200 / 2,617 | 148 / 105 ms | 7.2 | 1.64 / 0.88 |

The cache's lead is clear at every size: +17% to +24%.

- **Throughput grows with processes, but not linearly here,** and the table shows why: requests a second per
  gateway core fall from 623 at 1 worker to 310 at 8. All 8 workers share CPUs 0-7, which are only four physical
  cores. From 4 workers on, each pair shares a core's two hyperthreads, and a hyperthread is worth far less than a
  core. Containers on their own cores, or their own hosts, would scale better than this. This run can't show by how
  much.
- **The cache halves PostgreSQL's work.** At 8 workers it used 1.64 cores without the cache and 0.88 with it - most
  of PostgreSQL's load was QueryAPIGate's own store, not the queries.
- **p99 at 8 workers** rises because 8 processes, 64 callers, and the gateway's own threads all contend for 8 hardware
  threads.

### Threads per worker

One worker, the lookup, 32 callers, threads interleaved, 3 rounds:

| Threads | req/s | p99 | Gateway cores |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 778 (777-828) | 52.5 ms | 0.88 |
| 2 | 832 (831-902) | 49.1 ms | 1.12 |
| 4 | 763 (760-763) | 53.3 ms | 1.18 |
| 8 | 723 (722-725) | 56.4 ms | 1.20 |

A second thread helps a little: it runs Python while the first waits on the database. **Beyond two, throughput
falls.** Eight threads, the Docker image's setting, are 13% slower than two on this workload, because they compete
for Python's global interpreter lock - and, the profile shows, for the logging module's lock. Threads aren't for
CPU. They are for calls that wait: slow queries, `?stream=true` exports, and `/events` connections that stay open.
v1 said "they don't add CPU" and cited +42% from 1 to 2 threads. That figure came from the unstable laptop; this one
doesn't.

### The cold path: every 60 seconds

150 s of the lookup at 8 callers, each request's duration taken from gunicorn's access log (`%(D)s`):

| Key | Requests | p50 | p99 | p99.9 | p99.99 | Slowest |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| governed | 106,741 | 9.25 ms | 14.66 ms | 19.2 ms | 73.7 ms | 146.9 ms |
| plain | 115,314 | 8.58 ms | 13.57 ms | 16.9 ms | 20.9 ms | 26.0 ms |

- **The governed key's slow seconds come every 60 s:** t=1 (147 ms), t=61 (76 ms) and t=121 (74 ms). In a typical
  second, the slowest request takes 17 ms. Those are the moments QueryAPIGate re-reads the connection's schema and
  re-traces the statement for masking, which it does every 60 seconds.
- **Some callers pay for it:** the few that arrive while it happens wait about 60 ms more. It shows at p99.99, not
  at p99.9.
- **The plain key** has no table check or masking to redo, and no such spikes.

### The access log

`main`, the lookup, 32 callers, gunicorn's access log on and off, interleaved, 5 rounds:

| Access log | req/s | p50 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| on (the Docker image's default) | 736 (735-739) | 43.0 ms | 54.4 ms |
| off | 785 (782-792) | 40.2 ms | 51.7 ms |

**The access log costs 7%.** QueryAPIGate also logs two lines of its own for each request, at INFO, which can't be
turned off. The profile below puts all logging at a fifth of the gateway's CPU.

### A database across a network

netem on the database container delays everything PostgreSQL sends by 0.5 ms, which is a same-zone cloud round trip
(`tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 0.5ms`, ping 0.04 → 0.56 ms). The lookup, 3 rounds of 30 s:

| | v0.41.0 | main | Cached |
|---|---|---|---|
| One caller: req/s | 132 (132-134) | 161 (159-162) | 270 (268-270) |
| One caller: p50 | 7.63 ms | 6.24 ms | 3.69 ms |
| 32 callers: req/s | 677 (672-752) | 741 (735-750) | 860 (857-870) |

- **One caller pays for every round trip.** At 0.5 ms each, a call went from 1.4 to 6.2 ms on `main`. Fewer store
  reads made `main` 22% faster than v0.41.0. The cache made it 67% faster again, and halved single-call latency to
  3.7 ms.
- **With 32 callers, round trips overlap,** and the CPU is the limit again: the same order as without a delay.
  v0.41.0's range overlaps `main`'s here, because one of its rounds ran fast.
- This is a simulation: one-way delay, no packet loss or jitter. Read it as how many round trips a call makes, not
  as a cloud measurement.

### Mixed reads and writes, and hot rows

`main`, 3 rounds of 30 s:

| Workload | req/s | p50 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reads (24 callers) and writes (8 callers) at once | 547 + 181 = 728 | 43.3 / 43.6 ms | 54.8 / 54.9 ms |
| Writes on 10 million accounts (32 callers) | 734 (729-734) | 43.1 ms | 55.0 ms |
| Writes on 99 hot accounts (32 callers) | 735 (731-740) | 43.0 ms | 54.7 ms |

- **Mixing reads and writes changes nothing:** they share the process's capacity in proportion.
- **Writes on 99 hot rows cost the same as on 10 million.** One worker sends at most 8 at once, so PostgreSQL's row
  locks never queue long enough to show. With many workers, or a slow transaction, they would.

## Where the time goes

### Round trips per call

Counted exactly: `log_statement = 'all'` on each database, then 100 calls after a warm-up.

| Statements per call | v0.41.0 | main | Cached |
|---|---|---|---|
| Store, plain key or writer | 7: 5 reads, 2 inserts | 3: the key, the query, the connection | 0.1: history, in batches |
| Store, governed key | 8 | 4 | 1 - the masking hash key |
| Data database, any call | 4: `BEGIN READ ONLY`, `SET LOCAL statement_timeout`, the query, `ROLLBACK` | 4 | 4 |

- **History and events** are written in batches of up to 500 by a background thread, about once a second. That's
  about 0.01 statements per call in `main`, against one insert per row in v0.41.0.
- **The governed key reads the masking hash key on every call,** even with the cache on.
- **A query takes four round trips** to the data database: a transaction, its time limit, the statement, and the
  rollback (or commit, for a write). That's what the network test above measures.

### The CPU

py-spy at 200 samples a second across the worker's threads, during 30 s of the lookup at 32 callers. Each sample is
counted under the innermost frame that falls in one of these categories:

| Where the samples fall | main | Cached |
|---|---|---|
| Store layer: queries, decoding rows, checks | 28.2% | 13.4% |
| Logging: the access log and QueryAPIGate's own lines | 18.4% | 20.4% |
| gunicorn, sockets, HTTP | 16.8% | 21.0% |
| Data query: the driver and the pool | 12.3% | 15.4% |
| Flask and Werkzeug | 9.9% | 11.9% |
| QueryAPIGate's request handling | 4.6% | 5.6% |
| History writer thread | 3.0% | 3.7% |
| Authentication, limits, quotas, metrics | 2.5% | 2.8% |
| SQL checks, parameters, masking | 1.7% | 1.9% |
| JSON | 1.3% | 2.6% |
| Other | 1.3% | 1.3% |

The busiest single frames say more:

- **`logging` lock acquisition: 8-10%.** Eight threads write log lines through one handler, and wait on its lock -
  the same contention that makes more threads slower.
- **`store.refuse_store_access`: 7-10%.** A safety check that a connection doesn't point at QueryAPIGate's own
  SQLite file. It resolves file paths (`os.path.realpath`, several system calls) on every call - even for a
  PostgreSQL connection, which has no file to point at. With the cache on, it is the largest single cost in the store
  layer.
- **The store's `execute`: 17% in main, gone with the cache** - the three reads.
- **gunicorn's per-request worker heartbeat (`workertmp.notify`): 3%.**
